Cycles: the surviving path (lo != 0, hi == 0, the normal partial-clip case) goes 23 -> 20; the lo == 0 rejection goes 24 (or 19) -> 14; the one path that loses is lo != 0 with hi != 0, 19 -> 21, because it now pays 2 for a not-taken beq it previously skipped. That is the rect entirely off the left edge with a non-zero low sum, the abort case, so the trade is right. No labels added or removed.

assumption: LOUD FLAG: this rewrite DELETES one anonymous label (the ':' before 'lda gx0'). ca65 counts them, so every ':+'/':++'/':-' in level_init that counts past that line is silently retargeted. I checked the surrounding source: the only backward reference in range is the 'bne :-' of the gridsh shift loop, which names the ':' before 'asl' (after the deleted one), and the '@bx' block's 'beq :++' counts forward to ':asl' and ':clc', also after it -- so no reference actually moves. It must still be re-checked before applying. Also requires @nextobj to be within bcc range, which it is today since bcs reaches it.
original:
@box:   ; insert into grid cells gx0..gx1 x gy..gy1
        lda gy
        cmp gy1
        beq :+
        bcs @nextobj
:       lda gx0
        sta gx
proposal:
@box:   ; insert into grid cells gx0..gx1 x gy..gy1
        lda gy1
        cmp gy                      ; branch out iff gy1 < gy, i.e. gy > gy1
        bcc @nextobj
        lda gx0
        sta gx
argument: The original tests 'gy > gy1' with the two-branch idiom: beq skips the bcs so that equality falls through, then bcs leaves for gy > gy1. Swapping the operands turns it into a single unsigned test: 'lda gy1 / cmp gy / bcc @nextobj' branches exactly when gy1 < gy, i.e. gy > gy1, and falls through on gy <= gy1 -- the same partition, still an unsigned comparison on both sides, so the signed/unsigned rule is not violated (gy and gy1 are grid row indices, both compared unsigned today). Cycles: gy < gy1 was 3+3+2+2 = 10, now 3+3+2 = 8 (-2); gy = gy1 was 3+3+3 = 9, now 8 (-1); gy > gy1 was 3+3+2+3 = 11, now 3+3+3 = 9 (-2). Bytes: 8 becomes 6. Registers/flags: A holds gy1 instead of gy at the join, but the next instruction is 'lda gx0', so A is dead; X and Y are untouched by both forms; the carry left behind differs but the next carry consumer is the 'clc / adc gx' inside @bx, which sets its own. The one real hazard is the anonymous-label count, flagged above. Note the identical idiom appears a second time further down level_init (at the 'inc gy' loop back-edge) and could take the same treatment, but that is outside this window.

assumption: wfine is always 2, 4 or 6 (stated by the comment and by its declaration at engine.s:145, 'fine scanline offset 0,2,4,6' -- the 0 case is handled by the separate @all path at line 1892, which is why the window maps 2,4,6 only). X is free here: the original clobbers it with `tax` anyway, and nothing in the @fjmp loop body (the unrolled ldy/lda/sta groups, spnext, the ptr bump, dec cnt) touches X. If @ftab happens to land within 2 bytes of a page boundary the new base @ftab-2 could add 1 cycle to each of the two loads; align or pad if so.
original:
lda wfine
        lsr
        deca
        asl
        tax
        lda @ftab,x
        sta @fjmp+1
        lda @ftab+1,x
        sta @fjmp+2
@fjmp:  jmp @g2
proposal:
ldx wfine
        lda @ftab-2,x
        sta @fjmp+1
        lda @ftab-1,x
        sta @fjmp+2
@fjmp:  jmp @g2
argument: The index dance maps wfine 2,4,6 to X = 0,2,4 (lsr gives 1,2,3; deca gives 0,1,2; asl gives 0,2,4). Since wfine itself is already 2,4,6 -- the same sequence biased by 2 -- the identical word can be fetched with X = wfine and the table base biased by -2: @ftab-2+2 = @ftab (@g2), @ftab-2+4 = @ftab+2 (@g4), @ftab-2+6 = @ftab+4 (@g6). Cycles: original lda zp 3 + lsr 2 + dec a 2 + asl 2 + tax 2 + lda abs,x 4 + sta abs 4 + lda abs,x 4 + sta abs 4 = 27; proposal ldx zp 3 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 19, saving 8. Bytes: 18 down to 14. Flags: nothing between here and @g2 (`ldy #2`, which sets its own N,Z) reads the flags; both forms end with a `sta`, which sets none, so the live flag state at the jump is from the preceding `lda @ftab-1,x` / `lda @ftab+1,x` -- same kind of value, and unread. Registers: A ends as the patched high byte in both forms and is overwritten by `lda (sp),y` at @g2+2; X ends as wfine (2,4,6) rather than 0,2,4, which is safe because the loop body never reads X and the back-edge `bne @fjmp` re-enters below this code. Explicitly NOT proposed: replacing the self-modified `jmp @fjmp` with 65C02 `jmp (@ftab,x)`. @fjmp is the loop back-edge (`bne @fjmp` at the bottom), executed ROWCHARS = 80 times per call, and jmp (abs,x) is 6 cycles against jmp abs 3, so that would cost +240 cycles to save 16.

assumption: None for the rewrite itself -- A is written on both paths before it is used, and the branch target keeps its position in the anonymous-label count. Assumes no `:-` from below this point counts back to this particular label expecting it to sit on `jsr player_hit` rather than on the `sta`.
original:
stz hx+1
        lda facing
        beq :+
        lda #$FF
        sta hx+1                    ; facing left -> hx negative -> vx = +768
:       jsr player_hit
proposal:
lda facing
        beq :+
        lda #$FF
:       sta hx+1                    ; facing left -> hx negative -> vx = +768
        jsr player_hit
argument: The stz writes 0 and the taken-branch path wants exactly 0 in hx+1 -- and on that path A already holds facing == 0, because `beq` was taken. So one store serves both paths: sink it past the join. facing != 0: original = stz zp 3 + lda zp 3 + beq not taken 2 + lda # 2 + sta zp 3 = 13; proposal = lda zp 3 + beq not taken 2 + lda # 2 + sta zp 3 = 10. Saving 3 cycles. facing == 0: original = 3 + 3 + beq taken 3 = 9; proposal = 3 + 3 + sta 3 = 9. No change on that path, so the saving is 3 cycles when facing is non-zero and 0 otherwise. Bytes: 2+2+2+2+2 = 10 vs 2+2+2+2 = 8, saving 2. Flags entering jsr player_hit: original leaves N/Z from `lda facing` on the zero path and from `lda #$FF` on the other (sta sets nothing); the proposal is identical for the same reason. Anonymous-label count is unchanged -- the single ':' moves up by one instruction but is neither added nor removed, and `beq :+` still names it. Two further wins live in this window but are reported under logic_1047 (whose range also covers them): fusing `mov16 qy, py` + `add16i qy, 12` into a single add off py saves 12 cycles / 8 bytes, and the lda #$00 / sta vy half of `mov16i vy, -1280` can be `stz vy` for 2 cycles / 2 bytes.

original:
sta dpx
        and #$80
        beq :+
        lda #$FF
:       sta dpx+1
        lda dpx+1
        bmi @up
        bne @cdn                    ; >= 256
        lda dpx
        cmp #MAXDWY+1
        bcc @cdone
proposal:
sta dpx
        and #$80
        beq :+
        lda #$FF
:       sta dpx+1
        bmi @up                     ; A already holds dpx+1, with matching N/Z
        bne @cdn                    ; >= 256
        lda dpx
        cmp #MAXDWY+1
        bcc @cdone
argument: `lda dpx+1` reloads the byte that `sta dpx+1` has just written from A, so the value is already there; the only question is the flags, and they match too. On the positive path A is the result of `and #$80` on a value with bit 7 clear, i.e. $00 with Z = 1 and N = 0 -- exactly what `lda #$00` would set. On the negative path A is $FF from `lda #$FF`, with N = 1 and Z = 0 -- exactly what `lda #$FF` would set. `sta` disturbs no flags in between, and neither the deleted `lda` nor anything replacing it touches C or V, so the carry seen at @up and @cdn is unchanged as well. Both `bmi @up` and `bne @cdn` therefore read the same N and Z they read before. 3 cycles and 2 bytes, once per frame through vy_step. Anonymous labels are untouched. (Separately, and not proposed here: because dpx+1 is a sign extension it can only ever be $00 or $FF, which makes `bne @cdn` unreachable and the `cmp #$FF` at @up always true -- dead defensive code, but removing it is a redesign rather than a re-encoding.)

original:
stz hx+1
        lda facing
        beq :+
        lda #$FF
        sta hx+1                    ; facing left -> hx negative -> vx = +768
:       jsr player_hit
proposal:
lda facing
        beq :+
        lda #$FF
:       sta hx+1                    ; facing left -> hx negative -> vx = +768
        jsr player_hit
argument: The original pre-clears hx+1 and then overwrites it on one of the two paths, so hx+1 is stored twice whenever facing is non-zero. Moving the label so that both paths converge on a single `sta hx+1` stores it exactly once. Correctness hinges on what A holds at the join: on the taken branch `beq :+` means A = facing = 0, so `sta hx+1` writes 0, which is exactly what `stz hx+1` wrote; on the fall-through `lda #$FF` puts $FF in A, which is what the original stored. Crucially the branch must remain `beq` on facing itself - substituting A = facing for the constant $FF would be wrong for any non-zero facing other than $FF, and the zero path is safe only because beq implies A = 0. hx is zero page (hx = $D7, 2 bytes), so `stz hx+1` is 3 cycles / 2 bytes and `sta hx+1` likewise. Cycles: facing = 0 is 9 both ways (lda 3 + beq taken 3 + sta 3, versus stz 3 + lda 3 + beq taken 3); facing != 0 drops from 13 (stz 3 + lda 3 + beq not taken 2 + lda# 2 + sta 3) to 10. Saving 3 cycles on the facing != 0 path and 2 bytes always. Flags into `jsr player_hit` are unchanged: `sta` sets none, so on both paths the surviving flags are those of `lda facing` (Z=1, N=0) or `lda #$FF` (Z=0, N=1) exactly as before, and A is the same value too. Anonymous labels: one `:` before, one `:` after - the count is unchanged, only its position moves by two instructions, and no `:+`/`:-` reference crosses it (the `beq :+` that targets it is inside the window). The `lda health / bne @alive / jmp player_dead` tail is already minimal - `bne` cannot reach player_dead's destination as a single branch inversion because both arms end in `jmp`.

assumption: @out0 stays where it is (engine.s:1216). Mutually exclusive with the engine_1206 proposal, which relocates @out0 ~85 bytes further on and would put it 204 bytes away - out of branch range. The ':' line must be kept (see argument).
original:
lda (ptr),y
        sta sp_w
        bne :+
        jmp @out0                   ; (out of branch range on the 6502 build)
:       ldy #7
proposal:
lda (ptr),y
        sta sp_w
        beq @out0
:                                   ; keep the bare label: it preserves the anonymous-label count
        ldy #7
argument: The comment is stale - the Model B build was removed, so the 6502 range constraint no longer applies. From build/main.lst the jmp sits at 0x6E2 and @out0 at 0x759. After deleting the 3-byte jmp, @out0 lands at 0x756 and the branch's next instruction at 0x6E2, a displacement of +0x74 = 116 - inside the +127 limit with 11 bytes of slack. Cycles: the common path (sp_w nonzero) pays a taken 'bne' (3); the rewrite pays a not-taken 'beq' (2), so 1 cycle and 3 bytes. Flags/registers: A holds sp_w in both versions and the very next instruction ('ldy #7') resets N/Z, so nothing downstream sees a difference; the rare zero path reaches the same rts. Anonymous labels (rule 3): the ':' at line 1154 loses its only reference, so the label LINE must be left in place as a bare ':' - an unreferenced anonymous label is legal in ca65 and keeps the count intact for the 'bne :+' at line 1160 and every other forward reference in the routine. Confidence is medium only because the 11-byte margin is thin; ca65 would error loudly, not silently, if later edits grow the block.

assumption: X must be dead from the `pha` to the matching `pla`. Verified in the source: the matching `pla` is at logic.s:1380 (@acc), the only paths from here to it are lines 1364-1379 plus `bra @acc` at 1377, none of them contain a jsr, and none read or write X (mov16i is lda/sta only). @acc is reached from nowhere else. This fact is not visible inside the window, hence medium rather than high.
original:
pha
        lda running
        ora firing
        bne :+
        stz anim
:       ; accel = (alt > 0 || push == 3) ? 288 : 36
        lda alt
        beq :+
proposal:
tax                         ; stash the key bits in X, not on the stack
        lda running
        ora firing
        bne :+
        stz anim
:       ; accel = (alt > 0 || push == 3) ? 288 : 36
        lda alt
        beq :+
        ; ... and at @acc, `pla` becomes `txa`
argument: The `pha` here saves the masked key bits so that @acc can recover them with `pla` before `and #K_LEFT`. pha(3) + pla(4) = 7 cycles; tax(2) + txa(2) = 4, so 3 cycles go, at the same 2 bytes total. Flags: `pla` sets N,Z from the pulled byte and `txa` sets N,Z from X -- the same byte, so identical; the consumer is `and #K_LEFT` two instructions later, which sets its own flags regardless. Carry is untouched by all four instructions. Nothing in the window reads X, and the stack depth change is inert because every path out of the pha reaches the pla (the three `beq @norun` exits at 1358/1361/1363 all precede it, so there is no leak either way). Anonymous labels are unchanged. Caveat: this makes X live across a 16-instruction span, so it is worth a comment at the tax if adopted.

assumption: Master-only build (the comment's 6502 branch-range caveat no longer applies -- see the Model B removal). The displacement to @out0 measured 114-116 bytes forward, inside +127 but not by much; if a future edit pushes it over, ca65 raises a range error rather than mis-assembling.
original:
lda (ptr),y
        sta sp_w
        bne :+
        jmp @out0                   ; (out of branch range on the 6502 build)
:       ldy #7
proposal:
lda (ptr),y
        sta sp_w
        beq @out0                   ; zero width: nothing to draw
        ldy #7
argument: LOUD FLAG (rule 3): this deletes one anonymous label -- the bare `:` that currently starts the `ldy #7` line. The only reference to it is the `bne :+` being removed. I checked every anonymous reference in drawsprite (lines 1140-1500): they are all forward `:+`/`:++` binding to labels defined after them (1160->1162, 1210->1213, 1254, 1274, 1302, 1336, 1353/1355 the `:`/`:++` pair at 1356/1359, 1375, ...), and there is no `:-` anywhere in the routine, so nothing is retargeted; nothing before line 1152 has a dangling forward reference either. Correctness: `sta sp_w` sets no flags, so the Z consumed by the branch comes from `lda (ptr),y`, exactly as in the original -- `bne :+`/`jmp @out0` and `beq @out0` are the same predicate. Cycles: the normal path (sp_w != 0) pays `bne` taken = 3 in the original and `beq` not taken = 2 in the proposal, saving 1 cycle per sprite; the zero-width path pays `bne` not taken 2 + `jmp` 3 = 5 against `beq` taken 3, saving 2 there. Bytes: 2+3 = 5 becomes 2. Range: counting from the byte after the branch to @out0 at line 1216 gives 114 bytes with spclip zero page, 116 with spclip absolute (it is in the .res block at line 236, so absolute: 116). Registers and flags at @out0 (`rts`) are irrelevant. The rest of the window is already minimal: `ldaz ptr` (5) beats `ldy #0`/`lda (ptr),y` (7), and the `ldy #1`/`iny` walk over bytes 1 and 2 is the cheapest form.

assumption: For the ry rewrite: ry is not read between the mov16 and the sub16 (visible in the window). For the t16 rewrite: A and the N/Z/C flags are dead after 'asl16 t16' -- the next instruction is 'add16 t16, bvx', whose first two instructions are 'clc' and 'lda t16', so all three are overwritten before use.
original:
mov16 ry, py
        add16i ry, 8
        sub16 ry, by                ; ry = py + 8 - by
...
        mov16 t16, bvx
        asl16 t16
proposal:
clc                         ; ry = py + 8, built straight from py
        lda py
        adc #8
        sta ry
        lda py+1
        adc #0
        sta ry+1
        sub16 ry, by                ; unchanged
...
        lda bvx                     ; t16 = bvx * 2, shifted on the way in
        asl
        sta t16
        lda bvx+1
        rol
        sta t16+1
argument: Two independent local fusions. (1) mov16 ry,py (12 cycles, 8 bytes) followed by add16i ry,8 (18 cycles, 13 bytes) writes ry/ry+1 and then immediately reloads both to add to them. Feeding the add from py directly gives 18 cycles and 13 bytes for the pair instead of 30 and 21: 12 cycles, 8 bytes saved. The carry chain is unchanged (clc, low adc, high adc #0), py is unmodified between the two macros, and sub16 ry, by still reads ry/ry+1 so the intermediate must still be stored -- which it is. (2) mov16 t16,bvx (12 cycles, 8 bytes) + asl16 t16 (asl zp 5 + rol zp 5 = 10 cycles, 4 bytes) copies a pair and then shifts it in memory. Shifting in the accumulator on the way through costs lda(3) asl a(2) sta(3) lda(3) rol a(2) sta(3) = 16 cycles, 10 bytes, against 22 and 12: 6 cycles, 2 bytes saved. Correctness of (2): 'asl' on A sets carry from bit 7 exactly as 'asl t16' does, and the intervening 'sta t16' does not disturb carry, so 'rol' on the high byte shifts in the same bit. Flags at the end differ in one respect -- the original finishes on 'rol t16+1' (N/Z from the result) and the rewrite finishes on 'sta t16+1' with N/Z from 'rol a' on the same byte, so N and Z are in fact identical; carry is identical too. A differs (the shifted high byte rather than bvx+1), which is why the assumption above matters, and the source shows the next instruction is add16's 'clc / lda t16'. Registers X and Y are untouched by both rewrites. No anonymous labels are added or removed: mov16, add16i, asl16 and sub16 contain none, so the ':' before 'dif16' and the '@nocatch' branch targets are unaffected, and the ':+' of 'bcc :+ / jmp @bfly' still names the same line. Examined and rejected: collapsing the four ble16i/bge16i signed range tests on rx and ry into a bias-and-unsigned-compare would save roughly 7 cycles per axis but needs a scratch zp byte that the window does not name.

assumption: Nothing else falls into or branches to the instruction after 'sta control' expecting to reach @afterctl. Verified in logic.s: @setctl is entered only by 'bne @setctl' from the frame-difference test and by falling out of 'bcc @afterctl' not being taken; @afterctl keeps its label and its other entry (the bcc) is unaffected. Costs 2 bytes.
original:
@setctl:
        lda #1
        sta control
@afterctl:
        ; ---- choose sprite
        lda control
        bne @ctl
proposal:
@setctl:
        lda #1
        sta control
        bra @ctl                    ; control is 1: the test below can only branch
@afterctl:
        ; ---- choose sprite
        lda control
        bne @ctl
argument: On the @setctl path the code stores 1 into control and then immediately falls into @afterctl, which reads control back (3 cycles) and branches on it (3 cycles, always taken since the value is 1) - 6 cycles to rediscover something just written. A 'bra @ctl' costs 3, so the path saves 3 cycles at a cost of 2 bytes. Correctness: A at @ctl is 1 in both versions (original: reloaded from control, which was just set to 1; new: still 1 from 'lda #1', since sta sets no flags and changes no register). The flags at @ctl are also the same - 'lda #1' leaves Z=0/N=0, which is exactly what 'lda control' with control=1 leaves - and carry is untouched by lda/sta/bra in both. @afterctl is still reached by the 'bcc @afterctl' above, where control is genuinely unknown, so the reload must stay for that path. This is a cycles-for-bytes trade on a cold-ish path (control has just become 1), so it is a marginal call; it is unambiguously correct, just small.

assumption: That the animated frames (@f0/@f2/@f4/@f6, all of which reach @fr) are entered more often than the standing frame @f8. @f8 is reached only when fb is negative, zero, or >= fa, i.e. at the two ends of the walker's patrol, so this should hold -- but it is a frequency claim, not visible in the window. If @f8 dominates, the change is a 3-cycle loss, so it is zero-sum unless measured.
argument: Pure block reorder: move the one-instruction @f8 arm above @f4 so that @fr's 'adc fc' falls straight into @sp and the 3-cycle 'bra @sp' moves onto the @f8 arm instead. All four labels are named, so no anonymous-label counting is disturbed (rule 3 does not bite). Flags and registers are identical on both arms -- @f8 still arrives at @sp with A = 8 and @fr with A = frame + fc; the only flag consumer after @sp is well downstream and 'sta q1' sets none anyway. Cycle count is exactly conserved in total: the @f0/@f2/@f4/@f6 path drops from lda + clc + adc + bra + sta to lda + clc + adc + sta (-3), and the @f8 path rises from lda + sta to lda + bra + sta (+3). Byte count is unchanged. I also checked the tail of this window ('lda otype / cmp #5 / bne :+ / lda #67 / bra :++ / : lda #76 / : clc / adc q1'): hoisting the default with 'lda #76 / ldx otype / cpx #5 / bne :+ / lda #67' saves 1 cycle on one arm and 0 on the other, burns X, and deletes an anonymous label, so it is not worth it; and the obvious 'lda otype / cmp #5 / lda #76 / bne' is wrong because 'lda #76' destroys the Z the branch needs (rule 1).

assumption: r (= ringS - mulrowlo[barq], the char offset of the window start within its ring row) is < 128. By construction it is 0..ROWCHARS-1 = 0..79: barq is the ring row that contains ringS, and the routine's header comment defines r as wcx mod 80.
original:
sbc mulrowlo,x              ; r
        sta tmp2
        stz w16+1
        asl
        rol w16+1
        asl
        rol w16+1
        asl
        rol w16+1                   ; 8r
proposal:
sbc mulrowlo,x              ; r
        sta tmp2
        stz w16+1
        asl                         ; r < 128, so this shifts out a 0: nothing to roll in
        asl
        rol w16+1
        asl
        rol w16+1                   ; 8r
argument: The first 'rol w16+1' rolls the carry out of the first asl into w16+1. That carry is bit 7 of r, which is always 0 for r in 0..79, and w16+1 has just been zeroed, so the instruction is provably a no-op: it takes 0 << 1 | 0 = 0. Deleting it saves 5 cycles (rol zp) and 2 bytes. The remaining two rols still assemble the high byte correctly: after the second asl C = r bit 6, after the third C = r bit 5, giving w16+1 = r >> 5, which is exactly the high byte of 8r. A is unchanged (r << 3 mod 256) and is consumed by the 'clc / adc #<(RINGEND-ROWBYTES)' that follows, which sets its own carry, so no flag dependency is broken. tmp2 already holds r for the later MIRR_R comparison and is untouched. (An alternative that computes the high byte with five lsr's from tmp2 saves only 2 cycles and costs a byte, so this is the better form.)

assumption: LV_OBJS is page-aligned, i.e. <LV_OBJS = 0. Verified: engine.s line 68 gives LV_OBJS = $8100. Worth guarding with a `.assert <LV_OBJS = 0` so the build breaks if that ever changes.
original:
add16 t16, t16b
        add16i t16, LV_OBJS
        ldy #0
        lda (t16),y
        sta otype
        ldx obj
        sta O_TYPE,x
        iny
        lda (t16),y
proposal:
add16 t16, t16b
        lda t16+1                   ; <LV_OBJS = 0: only the high byte moves
        clc
        adc #>LV_OBJS
        sta t16+1
        ldaz t16                    ; lda (t16)
        sta otype
        ldx obj
        sta O_TYPE,x
        ldy #1
        lda (t16),y
argument: Two independent re-encodings. (1) `add16i t16, LV_OBJS` expands to clc(2)/lda t16(3)/adc #<LV_OBJS(2)/sta t16(3)/lda t16+1(3)/adc #>LV_OBJS(2)/sta t16+1(3) = 18 cycles, 13 bytes. Because <LV_OBJS is 0 and C is forced clear by the `clc`, the low-byte half computes t16 + 0 + 0 = t16 and provably cannot carry out, so it is a no-op and the high half reduces to t16+1 + $81 with carry-in 0. That is lda t16+1(3)/clc(2)/adc #>LV_OBJS(2)/sta t16+1(3) = 10 cycles, 7 bytes -- the explicit `clc` is mandatory because the preceding `add16` leaves C from *its* high-byte add, which is not guaranteed clear. Saving 8 cycles, 6 bytes, with a bit-exact result. (2) `ldy #0`(2)/`lda (t16),y`(5) = 7 cycles for the first byte; the 65C02 `lda (zp)` (the `ldaz` macro, already used throughout engine.s) is 5 cycles and needs no Y at all. Y is then set up for the second fetch with `ldy #1`(2 cycles / 2 bytes) in place of the `iny`(2 / 1). Net 2 cycles saved, 1 byte. Correctness: `ldaz t16` reads the same address as `lda (t16),y` with Y=0 and sets the same N,Z; `sta otype`/`ldx obj`/`sta O_TYPE,x` do not touch Y, and `ldy #1` leaves Y exactly where `iny` did (and the same N,Z from the value 1) -- and nothing between reads Y or the flags. No branches cross the region and no anonymous labels are added or removed. This runs once per object at level_init.

assumption: Y is dead between jsr ringaddr and the copy entry points (@g2/@g4/@g6 each begin with ldy #n), so it can hold the low byte. wfine is one of 2, 4, 6, which the original's own 'lsr / deca ; 2,4,6 -> 0,1,2' comment asserts.
original:
clc
        adc #<PARTADDR
        sta ptr
        lda ptr+1
        adc #>PARTADDR
        sta ptr+1
        lda ptr
        sec
        sbc wfine
        sta ptr
        bcs :+
        dec ptr+1
:       lda wfine
        lsr
        deca
        asl
        tax
proposal:
clc
        adc #<PARTADDR
        tay                         ; hold the low byte instead of storing it
        lda ptr+1
        adc #>PARTADDR
        sta ptr+1
        tya
        sec
        sbc wfine
        sta ptr
        bcs :+
        dec ptr+1
:       ldx wfine
        dex
        dex                         ; 2,4,6 -> 0,2,4
argument: Two savings. (1) ptr's low byte is stored and immediately reloaded only because A is needed for the high-byte add. Parking it in Y costs tay (2) + tya (2) = 4 against sta ptr (3) + lda ptr (3) = 6: 2 cycles and 2 bytes. The carry from adc #<PARTADDR still reaches adc #>PARTADDR (tay affects only N and Z), and sbc wfine / sta ptr / bcs are unchanged, so ptr and the borrow into dec ptr+1 are identical. (2) The jump-table index is lda wfine / lsr / deca / asl / tax = 11 cycles, 6 bytes, but ((w/2)-1)*2 is just w-2 for w in {2,4,6}. ldx wfine / dex / dex is 7 cycles, 4 bytes: 4 cycles and 2 bytes saved, producing the same 0/2/4. X carries the same value into lda @ftab,x; A is left holding ptr's low byte instead of the index, but the next instruction is lda @ftab,x, so A was dead. Flags after dex are N,Z from X as they were after tax. No anonymous label is added or removed - the ':' before the index code stays exactly where it is. Total 6 cycles, 4 bytes per partial-row copy.

assumption: None. LV_MAPROWLO ($A900) and LV_MAPROWHI ($AA00) are distinct pages, so the two stores are independent and may be reordered.
original:
ldx #0
:       lda t16
        sta LV_MAPROWLO,x
        lda t16+1
        sta LV_MAPROWHI,x
        lda t16
        clc
        adc t16b
        sta t16
        lda t16+1
        adc t16b+1
        sta t16+1
        inx
        bne :-
proposal:
ldx #0
:       lda t16+1                   ; high byte first, so the low byte is still in A
        sta LV_MAPROWHI,x           ; when the stride add needs it
        lda t16
        sta LV_MAPROWLO,x
        clc
        adc t16b
        sta t16
        lda t16+1
        adc t16b+1
        sta t16+1
        inx
        bne :-
argument: t16's low byte is loaded, stored, then loaded again three instructions later because the high-byte store sits between them. Storing the high byte first leaves A holding t16 across 'sta LV_MAPROWLO,x' -- sta sets no flags and does not touch the carry -- so 'clc / adc t16b' can run on it directly and the second 'lda t16' disappears. 3 cycles and 2 bytes per iteration. The loop is 'ldx #0 ... inx / bne :-', i.e. 256 iterations, so 768 cycles per call to init_maprows. Correctness: the two table writes go to different pages and neither is read by this loop, so their order is immaterial; the add16 that follows is byte-for-byte the same arithmetic on the same inputs; the loop's controlling flags come from 'inx', untouched. No anonymous label is added or removed -- the single ':' at the loop head and the 'bne :-' that references it both stay.

assumption: Nothing after the window reads V or C before the next flag-setting instruction - satisfied inside the window itself, where the next instruction is `lda rc_x` followed by `and #3`.
original:
sta rc_tx0
        lda w16
        sec
        sbc rc_tx0
        sta rc_nt
proposal:
sta rc_tx0
        eor #$FF
        sec
        adc w16
        sta rc_nt
argument: At `sta rc_tx0` the accumulator already holds tx0, and the very next thing the code does is reload w16 (3 cycles) only to subtract that same tx0 back out. Since sbc is defined as adc of the ones-complement, w16 - tx0 can be formed in place: eor #$FF (2) turns A into ~tx0, sec, adc w16 (3) gives w16 + ~tx0 + 1 = w16 - tx0. That is 7 cycles against 8 for lda w16 (zp, 3) / sec (2) / sbc rc_tx0 (zp, 3); bytes are 5 either way (2/1/2). Flags are bit-for-bit identical, not merely similar: the 6502 sbc is literally this adc, so N, Z, C and V all come out the same, and the result in A is the same value that is then stored to rc_nt. The three-instruction 16-bit >>2 above it (lda rc_x+1 / lsr / sta tmp / lda rc_x / ror / lsr tmp / ror) is already the cheapest form - X cannot substitute for tmp because the second shift must happen in memory while the partial result sits in A - and the (rc_x & 3) << 3 tail is 3 asls, cheaper than any branchless alternative.

assumption: None beyond the window.
original:
lda wy
        sec
        sbc maxwy
        lda wy+1
        sbc maxwy+1
        bmi @wyok
proposal:
lda wy
        cmp maxwy
        lda wy+1
        sbc maxwy+1
        bmi @wyok
argument: The low-byte subtraction's difference is thrown away -- it is overwritten by `lda wy+1` on the next instruction -- so only the borrow it produces matters. CMP is exactly that: it performs an unsigned A - operand with an implied carry-in of 1 and leaves C set iff wy >= maxwy, which is bit-for-bit the C that `sec / sbc maxwy` leaves. That is 3 cycles and 2 bytes (zero-page CMP; maxwy is in the .zeropage block at engine.s:207) against 2 + 3 = 5 cycles and 1 + 2 = 3 bytes. CMP leaves A holding wy rather than the difference, which is fine because A is immediately reloaded. CMP does not write V where SBC does, but V is never read here: the following `sbc maxwy+1` sets its own V and the branch is `bmi`, which reads N only. (This comparison is a sign-bit test rather than a proper signed compare, exactly as the codebase's own bge16 macro does it; the rewrite preserves that behaviour unchanged rather than fixing it.) This is precisely the shape bge16/blt16 already use -- `lda aa / cmp bb / lda aa+1 / sbc bb+1` -- so it also makes the hand-written clamp match the macro idiom. The same edit applies verbatim to the wx half twelve lines above, for another 2 cycles.

original:
mov16i vy, -1280
        lda #SFX_JUMP
        sta SFXREQ
proposal:
stz vy                      ; -1280 = $FB00: the low byte is zero
        lda #>(-1280)
        sta vy+1
        lda #SFX_JUMP
        sta SFXREQ
argument: mov16i expands to 'lda #<imm / sta dst / lda #>imm / sta dst+1' = 10 cycles / 8 bytes. The immediate is visible in the window: -1280 = $FB00, so the low half is 'lda #0 / sta vy' (5 cycles / 4 bytes) and the 65C02's 'stz vy' does it in 3 cycles / 2 bytes. Saving 2 cycles, 1 byte. Flags: in both versions the last flag-setting instruction is 'lda #$FB' (stz and sta set none), so N=1, Z=0 on exit either way - and the next instruction is 'lda #SFX_JUMP' regardless. Registers: A is clobbered in both, X and Y untouched. 'stz' is spelled plainly rather than via the stza macro because A need not survive here. No anonymous labels involved. The rest of the window is already minimal: 'bmi16 vy' is the cheapest 16-bit sign test, and rearranging 'lda alt / beq :+ / bpl @grav' only shifts cost between the zero and negative cases, which needs frequency data the window does not carry.

original:
mov16i vy, -1280
        lda #SFX_JUMP
        sta SFXREQ
proposal:
stz vy                      ; -1280 = $FB00: the low byte is zero
        lda #>(-1280)
        sta vy+1
        lda #SFX_JUMP
        sta SFXREQ
argument: -1280 is $FB00, so mov16i's low half is `lda #$00 / sta vy` - 2 + 3 = 5 cycles, 4 bytes on zero page (vy is at logic.s:216 in the .zeropage block) - where `stz vy` does the same job in 3 cycles and 2 bytes. Saving 2 cycles and 1 byte per jump. Correctness: STZ writes $00 to vy exactly as the load/store pair did, and it affects no flags, but no flag from the low half was ever consumed - the following `lda #$FB` overwrites N and Z immediately, and it is that load, not the stz, that sets the flags at the end of the sequence. So N and Z entering `lda #SFX_JUMP` are identical to before (and are overwritten there anyway). A: the original left A = $FB after the pair; the rewrite does too, since I keep `lda #>(-1280) / sta vy+1` in place. The order matters and is preserved: zero the low byte first, then load and store the high byte, so the last flag-setting instruction is the same one as before. The `@stand` arm's `stza vy / stza vy+1` is already stz, and `lda #1 / sta control` cannot share with it since A is 1 there, not 0.

assumption: A holds rc_tx0 at the 'sta rc_tx0' (it does - it is the value just stored). rc_nt is the only consumer of the result.
original:
lda rc_x+1
        lsr
        sta tmp
        lda rc_x
        ror
        lsr tmp
        ror                         ; A = tx0
        sta rc_tx0
        lda w16
        sec
        sbc rc_tx0
        sta rc_nt
proposal:
lda rc_x+1
        lsr
        sta tmp
        lda rc_x
        ror
        lsr tmp
        ror                         ; A = tx0
        sta rc_tx0
        eor #$FF                    ; A still holds tx0: w16 + ~tx0 + 1 = w16 - tx0
        sec
        adc w16
        sta rc_nt
argument: The tx0 computation itself is already minimal: two 16-bit right shifts with the high half parked in tmp costs 20 cycles, and the alternative form used for tx1 above ((rc_x_hi << 6) | (rc_x_lo >> 2)) needs six asl or three ror plus an and, costing 28 and 24 respectively. The saving is in the subtract. After 'sta rc_tx0', A still equals rc_tx0, so reloading w16 to subtract it back out is a wasted 3-cycle zero-page load. Two's complement: w16 - tx0 = w16 + (~tx0) + 1, so 'eor #$FF' (2) / 'sec' (2) / 'adc w16' (3) = 7 replaces 'lda w16' (3) / 'sec' (2) / 'sbc rc_tx0' (3) = 8. Bytes are identical (2+1+2 either way). Flags are identical too, not merely adequate: for a subtract done as add-of-complement the carry out is the same no-borrow flag sbc produces, and N, Z and V come from the same result - though it does not matter, since 'sta rc_nt' follows and the next instruction is 'lda rc_x'.

assumption: No caller of submin0 reads C or V afterwards. Verified: all six call sites (logic.s 549, 611, 630, 665, 731, 752) are immediately followed by 'lsr', which overwrites C, and none reads V.
original:
; A = max(A - n, 0)  (unsigned)
.macro submin0 n
        cmp #n
        bcs :+
        lda #n
:       sec
        sbc #n
.endmacro
proposal:
; A = max(A - n, 0)  (unsigned)
.macro submin0 n
        sec
        sbc #n
        bcs :+                      ; no borrow: A >= n, the difference stands
        lda #0
:
.endmacro
argument: The current form tests first and then subtracts unconditionally, so it always pays cmp + sec + sbc. Doing the subtract first makes the borrow flag itself the test. A >= n: sec 2 + sbc 2 + bcs taken 3 = 7 against cmp 2 + bcs taken 3 + sec 2 + sbc 2 = 9. A < n: sec 2 + sbc 2 + bcs not taken 2 + lda #0 2 = 8 against cmp 2 + bcs not taken 2 + lda #n 2 + sec 2 + sbc 2 = 10. Two cycles either way, and 9 bytes down to 7. Results are identical: when A >= n the subtraction is the same one; when A < n the old code contrived A = n so that sbc produced 0, the new code loads 0 directly. Flag difference, and the reason for the assumption: on the underflow path the old code ended with a subtraction of n from n, leaving C = 1 and V = 0, while the new code ends with 'lda #0' after a borrowing sbc, so C = 0 and V is whatever the real subtraction set. N and Z are the same ($00) on both. Every call site does lsr next, so C is dead at all six. Anonymous labels: exactly one ':' before and one after, and it stays at the same ordinal position relative to the branch that uses it, so no surrounding ':+' or ':-' reference is retargeted. The other macros in this window (bpl16, beq16, bne16) are already minimal - 'bit var+1 / bpl' is the cheapest 16-bit sign test, and lda/ora/beq the cheapest zero test.

assumption: No caller of submin0 reads C or V afterwards. Verified at all six call sites (logic.s 549, 611, 630, 665, 731, 752): every one is followed immediately by `lsr`, which overwrites C and sets its own N/Z. N and Z are preserved exactly by the rewrite in any case; only C and V differ, and only in the clamped case.
original:
; A = max(A - n, 0)  (unsigned)
.macro submin0 n
        cmp #n
        bcs :+
        lda #n
:       sec
        sbc #n
.endmacro
proposal:
; A = max(A - n, 0)  (unsigned)
.macro submin0 n
        sec
        sbc #n
        bcs :+                      ; no borrow: A >= n, result stands
        lda #0
:
.endmacro
argument: The original tests for the clamp, then substitutes n, then subtracts n from it to get zero -- doing the subtraction twice in the clamped case and paying for the test in both. Subtracting first makes the test free: `sbc` already sets C = 0 exactly when A < n (unsigned borrow), which is the same condition `cmp #n / bcc` was computing, so the clamp becomes a single `lda #0` on the branch. A >= n: sec 2 + sbc 2 + bcs taken 3 = 7 against cmp 2 + bcs taken 3 + sec 2 + sbc 2 = 9. A < n: 2 + 2 + bcs not taken 2 + 2 = 8 against 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10. Two cycles either way, and 7 bytes against 9. Result values are identical: A - n when A >= n, and 0 when A < n (the original reached 0 by computing n - n). Flags: in the A >= n case the exit flags come from the same `sbc #n` as before, bit for bit. In the clamped case N = 0 and Z = 1 both ways, but the original left C = 1 and V = 0 from its second subtraction while the rewrite leaves C = 0 and whatever V the borrowing `sbc` produced -- hence the assumption, which the `lsr` at every call site makes moot. ANONYMOUS LABELS: one `:` before, one `:` after, so the file-wide count is unchanged; note only that the label now sits at the end of the macro rather than in its middle, which matters to nothing since no argument of submin0 is an anonymous reference. The other macros in this window (bmi16/bpl16 as `bit var+1` + branch, beq16 as `lda/ora/beq`) are already optimal.

assumption: X is free at @spr. Verified: the only other entry is `@spr2: jmp @spr`, which arrives with X holding a discarded vx byte, and nothing between @spr and `jsr m_addsprite` touches X (mov16 is lda/sta only). q1 is read nowhere else in player_update - the only two references in lines 1470-1700 are this store and this load.
original:

        lda hurt
        beq @drawp
        lda frame
        and #3
        bne @boom
@drawp: mov16 spx, px

@spr:   tax

        beq @drawp

        and #3

@drawp: mov16 spx, px
        mov16 spy, py

        jsr m_addsprite

On the @boom path the id is simply abandoned in X rather than in q1; X is next written by `ldx #6` in the boomerang shift loop. addsprite clobbers X, which is fine because the value has already been consumed by `txa`.

assumption: None. (stz abs,x, opcode $9E, is a valid 65C02 form and is already used elsewhere in this codebase via the stza macro.)
original:

        sta SECTAB+4,x

        sta SECTAB+5,x

Flags: lda #0 sets Z=1, N=0 and stz sets none, but the very next instruction is 'lda #QVSYNC' which re-establishes N and Z, and nothing between reads them - so the difference is unobservable. A is not carried into the store of SECTAB+5 (that is an immediate load), so losing the $00 in A costs nothing. assumption: LOUD FLAG (rule 3): this DELETES one anonymous label (the ':' before 'stz fc'). In this region the labels are the one inside blt16/bge16's own expansion plus that one; after the change only the macro-internal one remains. I checked that no branch spans the region -- the surrounding uses are 'bmi16 fb, @bset' and '@draw: bmi16 fb, @f8', both named, and the file contains no ':+++' or ':---' anywhere -- but the count change must be re-verified against the assembled listing before committing.

        bmi @bleft

        bra @bset
:       stz fc
        bra @bset

        bmi @bleft
        ; bvx > 0: if B < A: C = 0

        bra @bset

The signed 16-bit comparison itself is untouched: both macros do the same cmp/sbc with the same V-correction, so the signed semantics are preserved exactly (rule 4) and 'fb < fa' still selects the stz. Cycles: the fb < fa arm was 18 (bvc taken 3, bmi taken 3) + 3 + 3 = 24 and becomes 17 (bpl not taken 2) + 3 + 3 = 23; the fb >= fa arm was 17 + 3 = 20 and becomes 18, so 2 cycles saved there and 1 on the other -- quoting 2. Bytes: one 'bra' (2) removed. Registers: bge16 clobbers A exactly as blt16 did, and A is dead at @bset ('lda #8' is the first instruction there). Flags: the only consumer was the macro's own branch.

original:
blt16 fb, fa, :+
        bra @bset
:       stz fc
        bra @bset
@bleft: ; bvx < 0: if B > 0: C = 1
        bmi16 fb, @bset
proposal:
bge16 fb, fa, @bset
        stz fc
        bra @bset
@bleft: ; bvx < 0: if B > 0: C = 1
        bmi16 fb, @bset
argument: The current shape branches over a branch: `blt16` jumps forward to the `stz fc` only when fb < fa, and the fb >= fa case has to spend an extra `bra @bset`. Inverting the macro removes that. `blt16 aa, bb, label` and `bge16 aa, bb, label` expand to exactly the same five instructions (lda aa / cmp bb / lda aa+1 / sbc bb+1 / bvc :+ / eor #$80) and differ only in the final `bmi label` versus `bpl label`, so the 15-cycle compare body is identical and `bge16 fb, fa, @bset` branches on precisely the complement of `blt16 fb, fa`. Cycles: fb >= fa was 15 + bmi not taken 2 + bra 3 = 20, now 15 + bpl taken 3 = 18, saving 2. fb < fa was 15 + bmi taken 3 + stz fc 3 + bra 3 = 24, now 15 + bpl not taken 2 + stz fc 3 + bra 3 = 23, saving 1. The trailing `bra @bset` after `stz fc` must stay because the @bleft block sits between it and @bset. Signedness is preserved - both macros do the full signed 16-bit compare with the V correction, so this is not the `cmp`/`bcc` unsigned trap. A and the flags at @bset are equivalent (both arrive from the same `sbc`/`eor` sequence, and @bset immediately does `lda #8`). `stz fc` still clears only the low byte of the 16-bit fc, exactly as before - the rewrite does not touch that. WARNING on anonymous labels: this deletes the `:` in front of `stz fc`. I checked logic.s 2618-2720 for backward references and there are no `:-` anywhere in ob_walker; every anonymous reference in the routine is a forward `:+`/`:++` resolving to a `:` that sits after this point (the pair near @sp), so nothing is retargeted. Confirm in the listing after editing. The saving is small, which is why I have marked this medium rather than high - it is correct, but it is 2 cycles in exchange for touching an anonymous-label chain.

assumption: tmp3 must be dead after the `cmp tmp4`. Verified for THIS copy (the @inside one): the remainder of mirror_run is `bcs :+ / sta tmp4 / : ldx tmp4 / beq @done / ...` and the @cp copy loop, which use only tmp4, w16, w16b, X and Y -- tmp3 is never read again. This does NOT apply to the near-identical block a few lines above (engine.s ~2157-2166), where `sbc tmp3` reads it back; leave that one alone. tmp3 is zero page (engine.s:134).
original:
lsr
        ror tmp3
        lsr
        ror tmp3
        lsr
        ror tmp3
        lda tmp3
        cmp tmp4
proposal:
lsr
        ror tmp3
        lsr
        ror tmp3
        lsr
        lda tmp3
        ror a
        cmp tmp4
argument: The block is a 16-bit logical shift right by 3 of (RINGEND - w16), with the high byte in A and the low byte in tmp3, after which only the low byte is wanted. The third round can be done in the accumulator instead of in memory: after the third `lsr`, C holds bit 0 of the twice-shifted high byte -- exactly what the third `ror tmp3` would rotate in. LDA affects N and Z only and explicitly does NOT touch C, so `lda tmp3` between the lsr and the ror preserves the carry, and `ror a` then produces the identical final low byte, in A, where the following `cmp tmp4` wants it. Cycles: original lsr 2 + ror zp 5, three times, plus lda zp 3 = 24; new 2+5+2+5+2+3+2 = 21, saving 3. Bytes: 9 + 2 = 11 down to 10. Flags: the original reaches `cmp tmp4` with N,Z from `lda tmp3`, the new one with N,Z from `ror a` on the same value -- identical, and cmp overwrites them regardless; C is set by the cmp in both. Registers: X and Y untouched; A holds the same final value. The only behavioural difference is that tmp3 is left holding the twice-shifted intermediate rather than the final value, which is why the liveness check above is load-bearing.

assumption: Nothing after the mov16i consumes A or the N/Z flags: the window shows 'bra @acc' then '@acc: pla', which reloads A and sets its own flags.
proposal:
lda #36
        sta t16
        stza t16+1                  ; was lda #0 / sta t16+1
        bra @acc
@acc288:
        mov16i t16, 288
@acc:   pla
argument: mov16i expands to 'lda #<imm / sta dst / lda #>imm / sta dst+1'. For imm = 36 the high byte is zero, so 'lda #0' (2 cycles, 2 bytes) + 'sta t16+1' (3 cycles, 2 bytes) can be the 65C02 'stz t16+1' (3 cycles, 3 bytes): 2 cycles and 1 byte saved. Registers: the rewrite leaves A = 36 instead of 0, but the very next thing on this path is 'bra @acc' and '@acc: pla', which overwrites A unconditionally -- and the 288 path already arrives at @acc with A = 1, so no code at or after @acc can have been relying on A. Flags: 'lda #0' sets Z=1/N=0 and stz sets none, but pla sets N and Z from the pulled byte and the first branch is 'and #K_LEFT / beq @right', which reads the and's flags. Carry is untouched by both forms. The 288 path cannot use the same trick (its high byte is 1). No anonymous labels change. Also examined: sub16/add16 vx, t16 on the two direction paths cannot share a single add by pre-negating t16, since that would cost a neg16 (16 cycles) to save nothing.

original:
lda tmp3
        sta w16
        sty w16+1
        lda w16+1
        cmp MIRR_LO+1
proposal:

        sta w16
        tya
        sta w16+1
        cmp MIRR_LO+1
argument: The code stores Y into w16+1 (sty zp, 3 cycles, 2 bytes) and then immediately reads the same byte back to compare it (lda zp, 3 cycles, 2 bytes). Routing it through A instead - tya (2 cycles, 1 byte) then sta w16+1 (3 cycles, 2 bytes) - writes the same byte to the same place and leaves A holding the same value the reload would have produced, for 5 cycles and 3 bytes instead of 6 and 4. Y is not modified by tya, so the later `sbc w16+1` and the mirror loop still see the same w16 pair. Flags: the original's `lda w16+1` sets N,Z from the value and leaves C,V; tya sets N,Z from the identical value and also leaves C,V; the following `cmp MIRR_LO+1` (MIRR_LO is in TABLES, absolute) then overwrites N,Z,C regardless, so the bcc/bne pair below is unaffected. Anonymous label count unchanged.

assumption: wfine is in 0..7. Confirmed 15 lines above in the same routine, which already writes `lda wfine / eor #7 / inca` to compute 8-f.

        lda #0
        sta SECTAB+2,x

        sec
        sbc wfine
        sta SECTAB+3,x
        lda #2
        sta SECTAB+4,x

        stz SECTAB+2,x
        lda wfine
        eor #7                      ; 7 - wfine, wfine in 0..7

First, `lda #0 / sta SECTAB+2,x` (2 + 5) becomes `stz SECTAB+2,x` -- stz abs,x is a 65C02 mode costing the same 5 cycles as the store it replaces, so the `lda #0` disappears outright: 2 cycles, 2 bytes. Second, `lda #7 / sec / sbc wfine` (2 + 2 + 3 = 7) becomes `lda wfine / eor #7` (3 + 2 = 5): for any value in 0..7 the complement within three bits is the same as 7 minus it, which is why the identical idiom already appears in this routine at the PARTCRTC duration computation. 2 cycles, 1 byte. The only behavioural difference is C: `sec/sbc` left it set, `eor` leaves it as `adc #8` from the entry-index computation left it. Nothing reads C before the explicit `clc` four instructions later (`lda ringS / clc / adc #ROWCHARS`), so that is harmless. N and Z after `eor` describe the same value `sbc` produced, and are dead anyway -- a `sta` then `lda #2` follow. X is untouched by both changes and still indexes the SECTAB entry.

assumption: A holds the value that was just stored (sta does not alter A), and @emit does not read N or Z on entry -- it is entered with `jsr` from two sites, one of which (@one) reaches it via `lda tmp4 / sta tmp2`, i.e. with N,Z from tmp4, while the fall-through site currently also has N,Z from tmp4. original:
sta tmp4
        lda tmp4
        sta tmp2
        jsr @emit

        sta tmp2
        jsr @emit

Deleting it makes the pair a double store, which is what the code means. Data flow is identical: tmp4 and tmp2 both end up holding A. The only observable difference is the flag state handed to `jsr @emit`, which is why this is medium and not high -- see the assumption. Note the other two occurrences in the window (`@one: lda tmp4 / sta tmp2` and `@past: lda tmp4`) are genuine loads: A has been clobbered by `jsr @emit` in both cases, so they must stay.

original:
tay
        ; dx = wcx - BUF_CX
        lda wcx
        sec
        sbc BUF_CX,y
        sta w16
        lda wcx+1
        sbc BUF_CX+1,y
        sta w16+1
        ; dy = wcy - BUF_CY
        lda wcy
        sec
        sbc BUF_CY,x
        sta w16b

        ; |dx| >= 80 -> full
        lda w16+1
        beq @dxpos
        cmp #$FF
        beq :+
proposal:
tay
        ; dy = wcy - BUF_CY
        lda wcy
        sec
        sbc BUF_CY,x
        sta w16b
        ; dx = wcx - BUF_CX
        lda wcx
        sec
        sbc BUF_CX,y
        sta w16
        lda wcx+1
        sbc BUF_CX+1,y
        sta w16+1

        ; |dx| >= 80 -> full  (A still holds w16+1, flags still from the sbc)
        beq @dxpos
        cmp #$FF
        beq :+
argument: The two subtractions are independent - dy reads wcy/BUF_CY,x, dx reads wcx/BUF_CX,y, and neither writes anything the other reads - so they can be swapped. Doing dx last leaves A = w16+1 and, because sta writes no flags, leaves the Z and N of the high sbc live at the test, so lda w16+1 (3 cycles, 2 bytes) is simply deleted. Registers: both X (curbuf) and Y (curbuf*2) are set before the block and neither subtraction disturbs them, so moving the dy subtraction earlier is safe; A is the only carrier and each subtraction starts with its own sec, both of which move with their subtraction, so no borrow leaks between them (in particular the dx low sbc still gets C=1 from its own sec, and the dx high sbc still gets the borrow from the low one - they stay adjacent). The test that follows reads only Z (beq @dxpos) and then A (cmp #$FF), both of which are exactly what the original lda restored. w16 and w16+1 are written before the branch, as before, and w16b is written earlier than before but by the same code - no path between the old and new positions reads it. No anonymous labels added or removed. Net 3 cycles, 2 bytes on every scroll_validate call.

assumption: curbuf is not modified by bar_bg (nothing in the window suggests it is - the existing comment says only that bar_bg clobbers X).
original:
ldx curbuf
        lda BARBG,x
        beq :+
        jsr bar_bg
        ldx curbuf                  ; bar_bg pages banks -> X clobbered
        stza BARBG,x
:       ldx curbuf
        lda BARDIRTY,x
proposal:
ldx curbuf
        lda BARBG,x
        beq :+
        jsr bar_bg
        ldx curbuf                  ; bar_bg pages banks -> X clobbered
        stza BARBG,x
:       lda BARDIRTY,x
argument: X already holds curbuf on both paths into the `:` label, so the third `ldx curbuf` is dead. Path A (BARBG,x was zero): `ldx curbuf` at the top loads it, `lda BARBG,x` does not touch X, `beq :+` does not touch X - X = curbuf. Path B: after `jsr bar_bg` clobbers X the code reloads it with the second `ldx curbuf`, and `stz BARBG,x` is a store that leaves X alone - X = curbuf. So both predecessors arrive with X = curbuf and the reload is redundant. curbuf is zero page (engine.s:146, inside the `.zeropage` block that runs from line 127 to the `.segment "TABLES"` at 219), so `ldx curbuf` is 3 cycles and 2 bytes. Flags: `ldx` sets N and Z from curbuf, but the very next instruction is `lda BARDIRTY,x`, which overwrites both before the `beq :+` that follows reads them - so removing it cannot change the branch. A is unaffected (`ldx` does not touch A, and A is dead here anyway: it held BARBG,x or nothing). No anonymous label is added or removed - the `:` line stays, it simply now labels `lda BARDIRTY,x`, so the `beq :+` above and the `:+` chain below are unchanged. Once per rendered frame, so 3 cycles a frame; small but free and risk-free. The identical pattern does not recur at the second `:` - that one is followed by `stza NSPR`, which does not use X.

assumption: None. A is dead immediately after the block (the next instruction is `lda wy`).
original:
lda wx
        sta wcx
        lda wx+1
        sta wcx+1
        lsr wcx+1
        ror wcx
proposal:
lda wx
        sta wcx
        lda wx+1
        lsr
        sta wcx+1
        ror wcx
argument: wcx+1 is written and then immediately shifted in memory. Doing the shift in A before the store gives the identical result and identical carry: `lsr` on A produces wx+1>>1 with C = bit 0 of wx+1, which is exactly what `lsr wcx+1` produced for the following `ror wcx`. Cycles: `sta wcx+1`(3) + `lsr wcx+1`(5) = 8 becomes `lsr`(2) + `sta wcx+1`(3) = 5, saving 3; bytes 2+2 = 4 become 1+2 = 3, saving 1. Flags on exit are set by `ror wcx` in both versions and are therefore identical. The only difference is A, which holds wx+1>>1 instead of wx+1 and is overwritten by the very next `lda wy`. The wcy block below cannot be improved the same way: the 16-bit >>2 genuinely needs a memory (or stack) temp to carry bit 9 across the reload of wy, because there is no way to shift X or to get a second carry out without destroying A - the current `sta wcy / lda wy / ror / lsr wcy / ror` is already the minimal form, and using X as the temp fails at the second shift.

assumption: None. Both predecessors of the `:` label are inside the window.
original:
lda BARBG,x
        beq :+
        jsr bar_bg
        ldx curbuf                  ; bar_bg pages banks -> X clobbered
        stza BARBG,x
:       ldx curbuf
        lda BARDIRTY,x
proposal:
lda BARBG,x
        beq :+
        jsr bar_bg
        ldx curbuf                  ; bar_bg pages banks -> X clobbered
        stza BARBG,x
:       lda BARDIRTY,x
argument: X already holds curbuf on both paths into the `:` label, so the reload is dead. Path 1: `ldx curbuf` at the top of the block, `lda BARBG,x` and `beq :+` neither touch X. Path 2: bar_bg clobbers X but the block reloads `ldx curbuf` before `stz BARBG,x`, and `stz abs,x` writes no register and sets no flags, so X is still curbuf at the label. The label has no other referents - it is the target of that one `beq :+`. Deleting the instruction saves `ldx zp` = 3 cycles and 2 bytes every frame. Flags: `ldx` was setting N,Z from curbuf, but the next instruction `lda BARDIRTY,x` sets its own N,Z and is what `beq :+` below reads, so nothing consumes the removed flag write. The `:` label simply attaches to `lda BARDIRTY,x` instead, so the anonymous label COUNT is unchanged and no `:+`/`:-` elsewhere is retargeted. The identical-looking `ldx curbuf` after `jsr t_redraw_hud` must stay - t_redraw_hud clobbers X.

assumption: None.
original:
lda tmp4
        sec
        sbc tmp2
        sta tmp4
        lda tmp4
        sta tmp2
        jsr @emit                   ; second part, read through the mirror
proposal:
lda tmp4
        sec
        sbc tmp2
        sta tmp4
        sta tmp2                    ; A is still the value just stored
        jsr @emit                   ; second part, read through the mirror
argument: 'sta tmp4' does not alter A, so at the following 'lda tmp4' the accumulator already holds exactly the byte that was just written -- the load re-reads memory for a value it is already holding. Deleting it saves 3 cycles and 2 bytes and leaves 'sta tmp2' storing the identical byte. Flags: 'lda tmp4' would set N and Z from the loaded byte; without it the flags in force are those from 'sbc tmp2', which set N and Z from the same result byte, so the flag state at 'jsr @emit' is bit-for-bit identical (carry and overflow are equally untouched by lda, so nothing changes there either). Registers: X and Y are untouched; A is unchanged in value. No anonymous labels are involved. The remaining instructions are all necessary: tmp4 must be updated in memory because the '@past' path below reloads it with 'lda tmp4', and tmp2 must be set because @emit reads it.

assumption: @dur preserves X and does not read or write SECTAB. Verified in engine.s:2486 - @dur is 'stza tmp3 / asl / rol tmp3 (x6) / sec / sbc #2 / bcs :+ / dec tmp3 / :rts'; it touches only A, tmp3 and the flags. The SECTAB slots written are all distinct (+0, +1, +6, +7 at the same X), so their order does not matter.
original:
lda wfine
        beq @coarse
        ; ---- f > 0 : T -> A (the partial row) -> P.. -> P2 -> Q
        lda #>PARTCRTC
        sta SECTAB,x
        lda #<PARTCRTC
        sta SECTAB+1,x
        lda wfine
        eor #7
        inca                        ; 8-f lines of it
        jsr @dur
        sta SECTAB+6,x
        lda tmp3
        sta SECTAB+7,x
proposal:
lda wfine
        beq @coarse
        ; ---- f > 0 : T -> A (the partial row) -> P.. -> P2 -> Q
        eor #7                      ; wfine is still in A from the test above
        inca                        ; 8-f lines of it
        jsr @dur
        sta SECTAB+6,x
        lda tmp3
        sta SECTAB+7,x
        lda #>PARTCRTC
        sta SECTAB,x
        lda #<PARTCRTC
        sta SECTAB+1,x
argument: 'lda wfine / beq @coarse' already leaves wfine in A; four instructions later the code reloads it with a second 'lda wfine' (3 cycles, 2 bytes) purely because the PARTCRTC constants were written to SECTAB in between. Hoisting the duration computation above those two stores lets the surviving copy in A be used directly. Saves 3 cycles and 2 bytes on the f>0 path. Correctness: the four SECTAB writes are to four different offsets of the same X-indexed record, so reordering them cannot alias; @dur is verified not to touch X or SECTAB (see assumption), so moving the jsr earlier is safe; 'eor #7 / inca' on wfine gives 8-f exactly as before (for f in 1..7, f^7 = 7-f, +1 = 8-f), and the f=0 case has already branched away to @coarse. The flags feeding nothing here: after the beq, A's N/Z are immediately consumed only by the eor's own result. Note 'sec / lda #8 / sbc wfine' would be the same 7 cycles and 5 bytes as the original reload form, so the reorder - not a different arithmetic idiom - is where the saving is.

assumption: A is dead after the loop -- the next instructions are `ldx #0 / lda #$FF`, which reload it. (If A were live the change would be wrong, since STZ writes a constant rather than the accumulator.)
original:
ldx #0
        lda #0
:       sta O_STAMP,x
        sta O_STAMP+256,x
        ... (eight more)
        inx
        bne :-
proposal:
ldx #0
:       stz O_STAMP,x
        stz O_STAMP+256,x
        ... (eight more)
        inx
        bne :-
argument: Honest but tiny. STZ abs,X exists on the 65C02 and is 5 cycles and 3 bytes, identical to STA abs,X, so the loop body does not get faster -- 2560 bytes at 5 cycles a store is the floor for an indexed clear, and there is no 65C02 block move to beat it. What goes away is the `lda #0` setup: 2 cycles and 2 bytes, once. Flags: `lda #0` set Z, but nothing between it and `inx` reads any flag (STA and STZ both set none), and `bne` reads the Z that `inx` produces, so removing the load changes no branch. X is still zeroed by `ldx #0` and the loop still runs the full 256 iterations. The preceding `dex / bne :-` and the `:` at the head of the window are untouched, so the `beq :++` further up (which the comment warns counts this `:`) still lands where it did: no `:` line is added or removed. Worth flagging only because it is free -- this is level_init, so the 2 cycles are paid once per level load.

assumption: Y must be free across @x8. Verified at all six call sites (@x8 is a cheap-local label, so level_init's are the only ones): logic.s:432/436/440/444 do not use Y at all around the calls, and logic.s:513/521 both reload it with `ldy obj` immediately after returning. Y is therefore dead across every call.
original:
@x8:    pha
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        tax
        pla
        asl
        asl
        asl
        rts
proposal:
@x8:    tay
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        tax
        tya
        asl
        asl
        asl
        rts
argument: @x8 turns a tile count in A into a 16-bit pixel count A/X = A*8, computing the high byte as A>>5 into X and the low byte as A<<3 into A. That needs the original A saved across the five lsrs, and the routine uses the stack for it. The Y register does the same job for less: `pha` is 3 cycles and `pla` is 4 (7 total), while `tay` and `tya` are 2 each (4 total), so 3 cycles go. Bytes are unchanged -- all four are single-byte implied instructions. The saved and restored value is bit-identical, so A and X on return are exactly as before. Flags: the original returns with N,Z from the last `asl`; the new version returns with N,Z from the same last `asl` (tya sets N,Z but is followed by three asls), and C from the last asl in both, so callers such as `sta startx / stx startx+1` see no difference. Registers: X is the deliberate second output and is unaffected by the change; Y is newly clobbered, which is what the assumption covers. Alternative encodings were worse -- building the high byte with stz/rol through a zero-page temp is 27 cycles against the present 25, and X cannot be shifted in place.

assumption: Saving is 8 cycles when the +4 does not carry out of O_XL (255 of every 256 values) and 2 cycles worse when it does; since the object X coordinates are arbitrary, expect ~7.96 cycles on average. Requires adding one anonymous label -- see the argument.
original:
@t1:    lda O_XL,y
        clc
        adc #4
        sta O_XL,y
        lda O_XH,y
        adc #0
        sta O_XH,y
        lda q1
proposal:
@t1:    lda O_XL,y
        clc
        adc #4
        sta O_XL,y
        bcc :+
        lda O_XH,y
        inca
        sta O_XH,y
:       lda q1
argument: The high byte is touched unconditionally by `lda O_XH,y / adc #0 / sta O_XH,y` at 4 + 2 + 5 = 11 cycles even though 255 times out of 256 the carry is clear and the byte is rewritten with its own value. Skipping the whole group on `bcc` costs 3 when taken, saving 8; when the carry is set the group runs as `bcc` not taken 2 + lda 4 + inca 2 + sta 5 = 13 against 11, costing 2. `inca` is used rather than `adc #0` because C is known to be 1 on that path, so the increment is exact and needs no carry input; note `inc O_XH,y` is not available -- the 65C02 has inc abs,x only -- which is why the value must round-trip through A. Flags: the original left N/Z from `adc #0`, the rewrite leaves them from `adc #4` or from `inca`, and neither is read -- `lda q1` follows immediately and sets its own. Y is unchanged throughout and still indexes the object slot. ANONYMOUS LABELS: this adds one `:` line inside @t1, which retargets any `:+`/`:-` that counts across it. I checked the neighbourhood: the anonymous labels in level_init are the dense single-step chain of `bne :+ / jmp @tN` dispatchers well above @t1, all self-contained, and the `:` inside the submin0 expansion four instructions below is created and consumed entirely within that macro and sits after the new label, so nothing in level_init is disturbed. Verify the assembly still builds and no branch moves before taking this -- and note that level_init runs once per level, so the practical value is close to nil; it is listed only because it is a genuine win.

assumption: Change is made at this call site only (logic.s:549), by expanding submin0 1 by hand; the macro itself and its other call sites (611, 630, 665, 731, 752) are left alone.
original:
lda q1
        submin0 1                   ; cmp #1 / bcs :+ / lda #1 / : sec / sbc #1
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        sta gx0
proposal:
lda q1
        beq :+                      ; submin0 1 open-coded: A=0 stays 0, else A-1
        deca
:       lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        sta gx0
argument: submin0 n computes max(A-n,0). For n=1 that is exactly 'leave 0 alone, otherwise decrement', which beq/deca does directly. Cost: the macro is cmp #1 (2) + bcs taken (3) + sec (2) + sbc #1 (2) = 9 cycles for q1>=1, and 2+2+2+2+2 = 10 for q1=0; the replacement is beq not taken (2) + deca (2) = 4, or beq taken (3) = 3. So 5 cycles saved on the common arm and 7 on the q1=0 arm, and 9 bytes (2+2+2+1+2) become 3 (2+1). Result is bit-identical in both cases: q1=0 -> 0 (macro: clamps to 1, subtracts 1); q1>=1 -> q1-1 with no borrow possible. Flags: the macro leaves N/Z from sbc and C=1; the replacement leaves N/Z from deca (same result value, so same N and Z) and C unchanged from whatever preceded. C is not consumed - the next instruction is lsr, which writes C itself, and nothing between reads it. Registers: A only; X and Y are untouched by both forms (Y is still the (t16),y index from the lines above, and neither version touches it). ANONYMOUS LABELS - worth checking explicitly: submin0 contains exactly one ':' (on its sec line) and the replacement contains exactly one ':' (on the first lsr), so the anonymous-label count through this point is unchanged and no :+ / :- elsewhere is retargeted. Separately, and not proposed here: the general macro would also be 2 cycles cheaper written as sec / sbc #n / bcs :+ / lda #0 / : - same single ':' - which would help the n=2 and n=4 sites.

assumption: Neither C nor V is consumed after the clamp - verified, the next instructions are lsr/lsr/lsr which overwrite C and then N/Z. The anonymous label count is unchanged (the macro contains exactly one `:`, and so does the replacement).
original:
lda q1
        submin0 1                   ; cmp #1 / bcs :+ / lda #1 / :sec / sbc #1
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
proposal:
lda q1
        beq :+                      ; max(A,1)-1 is A-1 for A>=1, and 0 for A=0
        deca
:       lsr
        lsr
        lsr
argument: submin0 1 computes max(A, 1) - 1, which for a byte is simply 'A minus one, but zero stays zero'. Its expansion costs cmp #1(2) bcs(3 taken) sec(2) sbc #1(2) = 9 cycles on the A>=1 path and 2+2+2+2+2 = 10 on the A=0 path, in 8 bytes. `beq :+ / dec a` costs 2+2 = 4 cycles for A>=1 and 3 for A=0, in 3 bytes: -5 cycles, -5 bytes. The values agree case by case - A=0 is left at 0 by the taken branch where the macro produced 1-1 = 0, and A>=1 is decremented identically. Flag differences: the macro ends with `sbc #1`, leaving C=1 (no borrow, since A>=1 was guaranteed) and V=0; `dec a` leaves C and V untouched and sets only N/Z, and the taken-branch path sets nothing at all. Neither matters: the three `lsr` that follow immediately overwrite C and N/Z before any consumer. This is the x0 = (q1-1)>>3 bounding-box clamp, so the result feeding the shifts is what must match, and it does. Only this call site changes; the submin0 macro itself is untouched for its other uses. The rest of the window (ldy #3 / three lda (t16),y / iny pairs) is already at the floor - explicit ldy #3/#4/#5 costs the same 30 cycles.

assumption: Y is not an input to ringaddr and is not read between @go and the later `ldy #2` (verified: ringaddr uses only A on entry and X internally, and never touches Y).
original:
@go:    sta tmp4                    ; first column to copy
        tay                         ; range is clean once copied
        lda #$FF
        sta PART_LO,x
        lda #0
        sta PART_HI,x
        tya
        clc
        adc wcx
proposal:
@go:    sta tmp4                    ; first column to copy
        lda #$FF                    ; range is clean once copied
        sta PART_LO,x
        stza PART_HI, x
        lda tmp4
        clc
        adc wcx
argument: Two independent tidy-ups. (1) `lda #0` (2) + `sta PART_HI,x` (5) = 7 cycles, 5 bytes is the 65C02's `stz abs,x` (5 cycles, 3 bytes) written long-hand: -2 cycles, -2 bytes. The only difference is that stz sets no flags whereas `lda #0` left Z=1, N=0; nothing reads them, because the next instruction reloads A. The codebase's `stza arg, ix` macro already emits exactly this form. (2) The tay/tya pair exists only to carry the column number past the two PART_ stores, but the same value is sitting in tmp4 and is reloaded from there a few instructions later anyway (`lda tmp4` before the shift chain). tay(2) + tya(2) = 4 cycles / 2 bytes versus `lda tmp4` = 3 cycles / 2 bytes: -1 cycle. `tya` and `lda tmp4` set identical N/Z (same value) and neither touches C, which is irrelevant here because `clc` follows. Dropping `tay` leaves Y holding whatever the caller left; Y is not read again until the `ldy #2` inside the unrolled line copy, and ringaddr in between neither reads nor writes it. @go is a branch target (`bra @go` from the dirty-column shortcut) which arrives with A = PART_LO,x; that entry contract is unchanged.

assumption: 12 cycles is the @c4 path. A second, independent 6-cycle saving on the mutually exclusive countdown path is described below; the two never both execute. @coll is already within branch range of both sites (the existing bne16/bra reach it).
original:
@c4:    mov16 t16, fa
        add16i t16, 128
        bge16 fb, t16, @coll

        ; and, on the other path:
        lda fb
        bne :+
        dec fb+1
:       dec fb
        bne16 fb, @coll             ; lda fb / ora fb+1 / bne @coll
        stza fc
proposal:
@c4:    lda fa
        clc
        adc #128
        sta t16
        lda fa+1
        adc #0
        sta t16+1
        bge16 fb, t16, @coll

        ; and, on the other path:
        lda fb
        bne :+
        dec fb+1
:       dec fb
        bne @coll                   ; dec fb already set Z from the new low byte
        lda fb+1
        bne @coll
        stza fc
argument: (1) The @c4 site is the same mov16-then-add16i pattern as logic_1670: copying fa into t16 (12 cycles, 8 bytes) and then reading both bytes straight back to add 128 (18 cycles, 13 bytes) totals 30 cycles / 21 bytes, where adding directly out of fa costs 18 cycles / 13 bytes. -12 cycles, -8 bytes. The carry chain is identical - clc before the low add, that carry feeding `adc #0` with only flag-neutral lda/sta in between - and t16 receives the same 16-bit value, so the bge16 that consumes it is unaffected. Note the immediate is 128, so `adc #<128` is `adc #128` and `adc #>128` is `adc #0`, exactly as the macro would emit. (2) On the countdown path, `dec fb` already sets Z from the decremented low byte, but the code throws that away and re-derives the 16-bit zero test with bne16's lda/ora/bne. Branching on the dec's own Z first and only falling through to test fb+1 when the low byte hit zero costs 5+3 = 8 cycles in the common case against 5+3+3+3 = 14: -6 cycles, and the byte count is identical (bne/lda/bne = 6 bytes, same as lda/ora/bne). The logic is equivalent because fb is non-zero as a 16-bit value iff its low byte is non-zero OR its high byte is; the original ORs them, the rewrite short-circuits. Neither form adds or removes an anonymous label, so the `:+` from `bne :+` above still resolves to the `:` before `dec fb`.

assumption: None. X is preserved by both versions and ptr/ptr+1 are the only outputs.
original:
txa
        lsr                         ; char = x/2
        stza ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
proposal:
txa
        and #$FE                    ; char = x/2, then *8 -- i.e. (x & $FE) * 4
        stza ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
argument: The sequence computes (X>>1)*8 as a 16-bit value in ptr+1:A. Shifting right once and then left three times is the same as clearing bit 0 and shifting left twice, so one asl/rol pair can be deleted outright. Algebraically (x>>1)<<3 = (x & $FE)<<2 for every x: x=5 gives 2<<3 = 16 and 4<<2 = 16; x=255 gives 127<<3 = 1016 and 254<<2 = 1016. The high byte agrees too - the original's three rols leave ptr+1 = bits 8..10 of a value that never exceeds 1016, so bit 10 is always 0 and ptr+1 = x>>6, exactly what the two remaining rols produce. Cycles: original `txa`(2) + `lsr`(2) + `stz ptr+1`(3) + 3 x (`asl`(2) + `rol ptr+1`(5)) = 28; new 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 x 7 = 21. Saving 7 cycles, and 13 bytes -> 11. Flags: both versions end on `rol ptr+1`, and the next instruction is `clc`, so neither the N/Z nor the carry left by the last rol is consumed. The discarded carry-out of the original `lsr` was likewise dead (the following `asl` overwrote it). A on exit is the same low byte in both, ptr+1 the same high byte, X untouched.

assumption: The proposal extends six lines past the stated window end (it rewrites logic.s:2915-2923, where the window stops at stza ptr+1 on 2917); the three asl / rol ptr+1 pairs it collapses are at 2918-2923 and are shown in full below. X is the bar column. No anonymous labels are touched. A is preserved into the clc / adc #<BARADDR that follows, exactly as before.
original:
txa
        lsr                         ; char = x/2
        stza ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        clc
        adc #<BARADDR
proposal:
txa
        and #$FE                    ; char*8 == (x & ~1)*4 : drop the lsr, drop a shift pair
        stza ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        asl
        rol ptr+1
        clc
        adc #<BARADDR
argument: The code computes char = x >> 1 and then the 16-bit product char * 8 in ptr+1:A. Because the shift right by one is immediately undone by the first of the three shifts left, (x >> 1) * 8 is identically (x & $FE) * 4 - masking off bit 0 is exactly what the lsr's discarded bit would have contributed, and (x & $FE) is at most 254 so it never itself overflows 8 bits. That removes one whole shift stage. The 16-bit result is unchanged in both halves: with c = x >> 1, the original leaves A = (8c) & $FF and ptr+1 = 8c >> 8 = c >> 5; the rewrite starts from 2c and shifts twice, giving A = (4 * 2c) & $FF = (8c) & $FF and ptr+1 = 8c >> 8 = c >> 5. Cost goes from txa(2) lsr(2) stz(3) asl(2) rol ptr+1(5) asl(2) rol(5) asl(2) rol(5) = 28 cycles / 13 bytes to txa(2) and #$FE(2) stz(3) asl(2) rol(5) asl(2) rol(5) = 21 cycles / 11 bytes - the win is one whole asl + rol ptr+1 pair, and rol on zero page is the expensive 5-cycle read-modify-write. and #$FE costs the same 2 cycles as the lsr it replaces. Flags: both versions end on rol ptr+1 leaving N/Z from that result, and both leave the product's low byte in A for the clc / adc #<BARADDR that follows; the clc means neither version's carry state matters. I checked the digit-tile computation just above (stz w16+1 / 5x asl / rol w16+1 / asl / rol w16+1) for the same trick and it does not apply - there the leading shifts genuinely discard bits 7..4 of a value that is already a single digit, and the only cheaper form needs a spare index register to stash the digit, which costs back what it saves.

assumption: A is dead after these macros (it already is - both forms leave a difference byte that no caller reads). The placeholder ':' in the proposal is essential and must not be dropped; see the argument.
original:
; branch if var < imm
.macro blt16i var, imm, label
        lda var
        cmp #<(imm)
        lda var+1
        sbc #>(imm)
        bvc :+
        eor #$80
:      bmi label
.endmacro
; branch if var >= imm
.macro bge16i var, imm, label
        lda var
        cmp #<(imm)
        lda var+1
        sbc #>(imm)
        bvc :+
        eor #$80
:      bpl label
.endmacro
proposal:
; branch if var < imm
.macro blt16i var, imm, label
        lda var
        cmp #<(imm)
        lda var+1
        eor #$80                    ; bias both sides by $8000 and compare unsigned:
        sbc #(>(imm) ^ $80)         ; the bias on the constant is free at assembly time
:                                   ; placeholder - keeps the anonymous-label count
        bcc label
.endmacro
; branch if var >= imm
.macro bge16i var, imm, label
        lda var
        cmp #<(imm)
        lda var+1
        eor #$80
        sbc #(>(imm) ^ $80)
:                                   ; placeholder - keeps the anonymous-label count
        bcs label
.endmacro
argument: Signed a < b is exactly unsigned (a xor $8000) < (b xor $8000). The low bytes are unaffected by the bias, so 'cmp #<(imm)' still produces the right borrow; the high byte needs 'eor #$80' on the variable at run time (2 cycles) and the same flip on the constant at assembly time (free). C clear then means signed less-than, so bcc/bcs replace the bvc / eor #$80 / bmi dance. Cost: 3+2+3+2+2 = 12 plus the branch, against 13 plus the branch when V happens to be clear and 14 plus the branch when it is set - so 1 to 2 cycles, and 14 bytes down to 12. LOUD WARNING, and the reason for the placeholder: the original macros each define one anonymous label, and this codebase branches across macro expansions with ':+' and ':++' (logic_2316 and logic_2542 in this same batch both do it). Simply deleting the ':' would silently retarget every such reference that counts past an expansion. The bare ':' line in the proposal keeps both the count and the ordinal, and keeps it immediately before the branch that takes the 'label' argument - so a call site passing ':+' as label still resolves to the same place it does today. If that placeholder is not carried through, do not apply this change. The two-variable forms (blt16, bge16, bgt16) get no benefit: biasing a memory operand would cost a load, an eor and a store. ble16i and bgt16i can be reduced to this same shape via var <= imm being var < imm+1, but that transform is not fully shown in this window.

assumption: Nothing between the stores reads flags: lda #0 currently sets Z=1/N=0 and the next instruction is lda #QVSYNC, which overwrites them. X is unchanged by stz abs,x.
original:
lda #0
        sta SECTAB+4,x
proposal: stz SECTAB+4,x
argument: 65C02 stz abs,x ($9E) is 5 cy / 3 bytes against lda #0 (2) + sta abs,x (5) = 7 cy / 5 bytes. Only the #0 entry qualifies; the other seven stores carry non-zero (or unknown-valued) constants, and no two adjacent constants are provably equal from the window, so no lda can be shared.

assumption: The value being formed is 8r with r a character index, so before the final rol w16+1 the high byte is at most 3 and its bit 7 is 0; the rol therefore always leaves C=0. Requires only r < 8192, which the surrounding ring geometry guarantees, but the instructions that build w16 are above the window.
original:
asl
        rol w16+1                   ; 8r
        clc
        adc #<(RINGEND-ROWBYTES)
proposal:
asl
        rol w16+1                   ; 8r  (C=0 out: bit15 of 4r is always clear)
        adc #<(RINGEND-ROWBYTES)
argument: rol w16+1 shifts out bit 7 of the pre-shift high byte, i.e. bit 15 of 4r. For any plausible column index that bit is clear, so the carry entering the add is already 0 and the clc is dead. 2 cy / 1 byte.
