The second `lda fa` exists only to restore a Z flag that `ldx #2` destroyed -- the comment on that line says exactly that. But `ldx` does not touch A: A has held fa continuously since the first `lda fa`, so the value need not be reloaded, only re-tested. `cmp #0` (2 cycles, 2 bytes) sets Z from A - 0 and N from A, which is what `lda fa` (3 cycles, 2 bytes) set, for 1 cycle less and the same size. The one difference is C, which cmp forces to 1; the join at @fr begins `txa / clc / adc #54`, so C is written before it is read and the change is inert. V is untouched by both. X is unaffected (still 0, 2 or 4 on the three paths), Y (the object index) is untouched, and no anonymous label is added or removed.

A larger restructuring is possible but I do not recommend it: `lda fa / bmi @f0 / beq @f2 / ldx #4 / bra @fr / @f0: ldx #0 / bra @fr / @f2: ldx #2 / @fr: txa` saves 4 cycles when fa > 0 and 5 when fa == 0, but costs 3 when fa < 0 and needs two new named labels. Note also the two dead ends I checked and rejected: `ldx #4 / bne @fr / ldx #2` does not work, because `ldx #4` sets Z=0 and the bne is therefore unconditional, giving X=4 for fa == 0 as well; and symmetrically, testing zero first and then the sign fails because `ldx #0` clears N. No register load on the 65C02 preserves the flags of a previous load, so the tests cannot be separated from the X loads without either a reload or extra branches.

assumption: t16 is a 2-byte zero-page temp (logic.s:280, t16 = $D1) and fa/fb are 2-byte zero-page object fields, so every lda/sta here is 3 cycles. Nothing between the writes and the reads named below touches t16.
original:
@dead:  ; falling
        mov16 t16, fb
        add16i t16, 256
        blt16 fd, t16, :+
        jmp @done
:
        add16i fa, 120
        mov16 t16, fa
        add16i t16, 128
        lda t16+1
        sx16 t16
        add16 fd, t16
proposal:
@dead:  ; falling
        lda fb                      ; t16 = fb + 256
        sta t16
        lda fb+1
        inca
        sta t16+1
        blt16 fd, t16, :+
        jmp @done
:
        add16i fa, 120
        lda fa                      ; A = high byte of (fa + 128); t16's own copy is dead
        cmp #128                    ; C = (fa >= 128), the carry adc #128 would make
        lda fa+1
        adc #0
        sx16 t16
        add16 fd, t16
argument:
Two independent dead-work eliminations, both entirely inside the window.

(1) `mov16 t16, fb / add16i t16, 256` is 12 + 18 = 30 cycles and 21 bytes, but adding 256 only ever touches the high byte: add16i's `clc / lda t16 / adc #<256 / sta t16` adds literal zero with C=0 and stores back what it loaded. Fusing the move and the add gives `lda fb / sta t16 / lda fb+1 / inca / sta t16+1` = 14 cycles, 9 bytes. `inc a` wraps $FF to $00 exactly as `adc #1` with C=0 does, and the carry out that adc would produce is discarded in the original anyway. Flags: both versions leave N,Z from the same high-byte result; the original also leaves C from that adc, but the next instruction is blt16, whose `lda fd / cmp t16` sets C itself, so C is dead. Saving: 16 cycles, 12 bytes.

(2) `mov16 t16, fa / add16i t16, 128 / lda t16+1` is 12 + 18 + 3 = 33 cycles and 23 bytes, and every byte it writes to t16 is dead. t16's low byte is overwritten two instructions later by sx16's `sta t16`; t16's high byte is read exactly once, by the `lda t16+1` on the next line, and then overwritten by sx16's `sta t16+1`. So the whole sequence exists only to leave (fa + 128) >> 8 in A. That is `lda fa / cmp #128 / lda fa+1 / adc #0` = 10 cycles, 8 bytes: `cmp #128` sets C=1 iff fa >= 128 unsigned, which is precisely the carry `clc / adc #128` produces, at 2 cycles instead of 4, and `lda fa+1 / adc #0` then forms the high byte. Flags entering sx16 are identical (the original's `lda t16+1` set N,Z from the same value, and C came from the same adc #0). sx16 reads only A. Saving: 23 cycles, 15 bytes.

Anonymous labels: unchanged. The `:` after `jmp @done` and the one inside blt16's own expansion are both untouched, and neither rewrite adds or removes a `:` -- which is also why I have left `add16i fa, 120` alone: turning it into `lda fa / clc / adc #120 / sta fa / bcc :+ / inc fa+1 / :` would save another 5 cycles on the no-carry path but inserts an anonymous label into a region where blt16 and bgt16 expansions are counting them. Registers: A is the only one used; X and Y (Y is the object index) are untouched throughout. This is the ob_bat death path, so the win is cold -- but it is 39 cycles and 27 bytes for free.

assumption: C and V are dead after the expansion - verified, the next instruction is 'lsr'. A is the only register involved.
original:
lda q2
        submin0 1
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        sta gy
proposal:
lda q2
        beq :+                      ; submin0 1 specialised: max(q2-1, 0)
        dec a
:       lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        sta gy
argument: For n = 1 the general macro is far more machinery than the case needs. submin0 1 expands to cmp #1 (2) / bcs :+ (3 taken) / sec (2) / sbc #1 (2) = 9 cycles for q2 >= 1, and 10 for q2 = 0. Testing for zero directly is 'beq :+' (2 not taken) + 'dec a' (2) = 4 for q2 >= 1, and 3 for q2 = 0 - saving 5 and 7 respectively, and 9 bytes down to 3. Correctness: q2 = 0 leaves A = 0, which is max(0-1, 0); q2 >= 1 gives q2-1 with no borrow possible. Flags: the old form ended with sbc, leaving C = 1 and N/Z from the difference; the new form ends with 'dec a' (N/Z from the difference, C untouched) or with the taken beq. The three lsr that follow overwrite C, and nothing reads N or Z, so only the value matters. Anonymous labels: submin0 defines exactly one ':', and so does the replacement, at the same ordinal - no surrounding reference is retargeted. This is a per-call-site specialisation and is independent of, and larger than, the general submin0 rewrite proposed for logic_164; the same form applies to the 'submin0 1' at logic.s 549 and 611.

assumption: X is not live out of this sequence. Verified in the window: X is set only to 0/2/4 and consumed immediately by 'txa'; what follows (bgt16, inc q1, mov16, add16, lda q1, jsr m_addsprite) never reads X. The proposal leaves X untouched instead, which is strictly less constrained.
original:
ldx #0
        lda fa
        bmi @fr
        ldx #2
        lda fa                      ; the ldx above set Z from 2, not from A
        beq @fr
        ldx #4
@fr:    txa
        clc
        adc #54
        sta q1
argument: The whole X ladder exists only because 'ldx #2' clobbers the Z from the first 'lda fa', forcing a second 3-cycle load - the comment in the source says exactly this. Deciding the value before committing it to a register removes both the reload and the txa/clc/adc that converts an index into a constant: N and Z from a single 'lda fa' distinguish all three cases. fa > 0: lda 3 + bmi not taken 2 + beq not taken 2 + lda #58 2 + sta 3 = 12 against ldx 2 + lda 3 + bmi 2 + ldx 2 + lda 3 + beq 2 + ldx 2 + txa 2 + clc 2 + adc 2 + sta 3 = 25, saving 13. fa = 0: 3+2+3+2+3+3 = 16 against 24, saving 8. fa < 0: 3+3+2+3+3 = 14 against 17, saving 3. The constants 54/56/58 are exactly what 'clc / adc #54' produced from X = 0/2/4, folded at assembly time, so q1 is identical on every path. Only named labels are added, so anonymous-label counting is untouched. I have quoted the fa = 0 figure as a middle estimate; which arm is hottest is not visible in the window, which is why this is medium and not high. The 'bgt16 ox, px, :+ / bra :++ / : inc q1' below could also lose its 'bra' by using 'bge16 px, ox' to skip the inc instead, but that would delete one of the two anonymous labels at the call site and retarget anything counting past them, for about 3 cycles - not worth it.

assumption: t16's low byte may be left stale between the two asr16 fusions - verified safe in the window, since each use is immediately followed by 'mov16 t16, <next>' which rewrites both bytes, and the final add16 consumes its value before any further use. Decimal mode clear, as the existing add16/add16i already assume. fa, fc, fd, t16, spx, spy are all zero page (confirmed).
original:
add16i fa, 120
        mov16 t16, fa
        add16i t16, 128
        lda t16+1
        sx16 t16
        add16 fd, t16
        mov16 t16, fc
        asr16 t16
        add16 spx, t16
        mov16 t16, fd
        asr16 t16
        add16 spy, t16
proposal:
add16i fa, 120
        lda fa                      ; want only the high byte of fa + 128
        cmp #$80                    ; C = carry out of fa_lo + 128
        lda fa+1
        adc #0
        sx16 t16
        add16 fd, t16
        lda fc+1                    ; t16 = fc >> 1 (arith), folded into the add
        cmp #$80
        ror a
        sta t16+1
        lda fc
        ror a
        clc
        adc spx
        sta spx
        lda spx+1
        adc t16+1
        sta spx+1
        lda fd+1                    ; same again for fd into spy
        cmp #$80
        ror a
        sta t16+1
        lda fd
        ror a
        clc
        adc spy
        sta spy
        lda spy+1
        adc t16+1
        sta spy+1
argument: Three independent fusions. (1) 'mov16 t16,fa / add16i t16,128 / lda t16+1' materialises a full 16-bit sum in t16 and then keeps only its high byte - and both halves of t16 are overwritten by the sx16 two instructions later, so the entire 16-bit value is dead. 'cmp #$80' sets C exactly when fa_lo + 128 carries (fa_lo >= 128), so 'lda fa+1 / adc #0' is that high byte directly: 3+2+3+2 = 10 against 12 + 18 + 3 = 33, saving 23 cycles and 15 bytes. The 'lda fa' reload is necessary because add16i above left the high byte of fa in A, not the low. sx16 then behaves exactly as before. (2) and (3) 'mov16 t16,X / asr16 t16 / add16 spx,t16' copies, shifts in memory, then adds back: 12 + 15 + 20 = 47 cycles. Done in the accumulator it is 31. Trace: 'cmp #$80' puts the sign bit of the high byte into C, 'ror a' makes that an arithmetic shift and leaves C = the high byte's bit 0, which the second 'ror a' feeds into bit 7 of the low result - identical to what asr16 computes; the high result is parked in t16+1 (the only temp still needed) while the low result goes straight into the add, with 'clc' discarding the stray carry the second ror produced. 16 cycles and 8 bytes each. Anonymous labels: mov16, add16i, add16 and asr16 contain none, and sx16's single ':' is preserved, so the count is unchanged - which matters here, because the 'bgt16 spx, px, :+ / bra :++' a few lines later counts anonymous labels across the expansions. Registers: A only; X is loaded ('ldx #65') after this block.

assumption: None.
original:
lda #<$0400
        sta ptr
        lda #>$0400
        sta ptr+1
        lda #0
:       sta (ptr),y
proposal:
stz ptr                     ; <$0400 is 0
        lda #>$0400
        sta ptr+1
        lda #0
:       sta (ptr),y
argument: <$0400 is $00, so 'lda #<$0400 / sta ptr' (2+3) is 'stz ptr' (3). The 'lda #0' three instructions later is still needed - it supplies the fill byte for 'sta (ptr),y' - and it re-establishes the N and Z that stz does not set, before anything reads them. The intervening 'lda #>$0400' means no attempt to share the zero between the pointer setup and the fill value is possible. Y is 0 on entry from the loop above and stz does not disturb it. Two cycles and two bytes, in a routine that runs once at startup - correct but near-worthless; noted for completeness. The SPRREC copy loop above is already the right shape: two lda/sta pairs sharing one iny/bne over 256 iterations.

assumption: Carry must not be live out of the clamp; here the next instruction is 'lsr', which overwrites C, so it is safe. Same site-local caveat as logic_623.
original:
lda q2
        submin0 1                   ; = cmp #1 / bcs :+ / lda #1 / : sec / sbc #1
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        sta gy
proposal:
lda q2
        sec
        sbc #1
        bcs :+
        lda #0
:
        lsr
        lsr
        lsr
        sta gy
argument: Identical transform to logic_623: subtract first, clamp the result, rather than clamp the input and subtract unconditionally. 'sec / sbc #1' leaves C = 1 exactly when q2 >= 1 (the same unsigned relation 'cmp #1 / bcs' tested, rule 4 respected), so 'bcs :+' keeps q2-1 and the fall-through substitutes 0. Cycles 9 -> 7 when q2 >= 1 and 10 -> 8 when q2 == 0, a flat 2 either way; bytes 9 -> 7. The anonymous-label count is unchanged at one, so no surrounding ':+'/':-' is retargeted -- note in particular the ':' a few lines above ('inc t16b / bne :+ / inc t16b+1 / : jsr mod16') is a separate, earlier label and is unaffected. The only flag difference is C on the q2 == 0 arm (0 instead of 1), immediately overwritten by the following 'lsr'.

assumption: LOUD FLAG (rule 3): this DELETES one anonymous label (the ':' before 'inc q1'). The region goes from three ':' (one inside bgt16's expansion, one before 'inc q1', one before the mov16) to two. I verified nothing branches across it -- the neighbouring anonymous references are all inside their own macro expansions or in the separate '@knocked' block below, and the file uses nothing deeper than ':++' -- but re-check the assembled listing before committing.
original:
bgt16 ox, px, :+
        bra :++
:       inc q1
:       mov16 spy, oy
proposal:
bge16 px, ox, :+
        inc q1
:       mov16 spy, oy
argument: bgt16 ox, px branches when ox > px; its complement is ox <= px, i.e. px >= ox, which is exactly bge16 px, ox. The two macros expand to the same six instructions (lda / cmp / lda / sbc / bvc :+ / eor #$80) with bmi against bpl, so the signed 16-bit comparison and its V-correction are unchanged (rule 4) -- only the operand order and branch polarity move, and swapping the operands is what turns 'greater than' into 'greater than or equal' with the sides exchanged. Inverting the sense lets the branch skip the 'inc q1' directly, which deletes the 'bra :++'. Cycles: the ox > px arm was 18 + 5 = 23 and becomes 17 + 5 = 22; the ox <= px arm was 17 + 3 = 20 and becomes 18, saving 2 there and 1 on the other -- quoting 2. Bytes: one 'bra' (2) removed. Registers: bge16 clobbers A exactly as bgt16 did, and A is reloaded by 'lda q1' before 'jsr m_addsprite'; q1 itself is untouched by either macro. Cost rank is 0, so this is correctness-neutral tidying rather than a performance win.

assumption: LOUD FLAG (rule 3): this DELETES one anonymous label (the ':' before 'ldx #66'), taking the region from three ':' to two. The only other anonymous label nearby is the one after 'jmp @done' near '@dead', which is above and outside; nothing after ':  txa' uses ':-' (the next thing is '@done: rts' and then the batoff table). Re-check the listing before committing.
original:
ldx #65
        bgt16 spx, px, :+
        bra :++
:       ldx #66
:       txa
        jmp m_addsprite
proposal:
ldx #65
        bge16 px, spx, :+
        ldx #66
:       txa
        jmp m_addsprite
argument: Same inversion as logic_2324. bgt16 spx, px selects X = 66 when spx > px and leaves X = 65 otherwise; bge16 px, spx branches when px >= spx, i.e. when spx <= px, which is precisely the 'leave X = 65' case, so the mapping is identical. Both macros expand to lda / cmp / lda / sbc / bvc :+ / eor #$80 followed by bmi or bpl, so the signed compare is unchanged. Removing the 'bra :++' costs nothing because the branch now jumps over the 'ldx #66' itself. Cycles: spx > px goes 20 -> 19, spx <= px goes 20 -> 18. Bytes: 2 saved. Rule 1 check: 'ldx #65' must stay BEFORE the comparison, as it does in both versions -- ldx sets N and Z, so moving it after the macro would destroy the sign bit the branch reads. Rule 2 check: the macro clobbers A, which is fine because A is only produced afterwards by 'txa'; X survives the macro untouched in both versions. Cost rank is 0, so this is tidying, not a measurable win.

assumption: None. Note this is once-per-boot code (cost rank 0), so the 2 cycles are of no practical value -- reported only because the rewrite is unambiguously correct and strictly smaller.
original:
lda #<$0400
        sta ptr
        lda #>$0400
        sta ptr+1
        lda #0
:       sta (ptr),y                 ; (Y is 0 from the loop above and stays there)
proposal:
stz ptr
        lda #>$0400
        sta ptr+1
        lda #0
:       sta (ptr),y                 ; (Y is 0 from the loop above and stays there)
argument: <$0400 is 0, so 'lda #<$0400 / sta ptr' (2+3 = 5 cycles, 4 bytes) is exactly what the 65C02's 'stz ptr' does in 3 cycles and 2 bytes. stz sets no flags, and none are live across it -- the following 'lda #>$0400' sets its own, and the loop's own 'lda #0' still supplies the A = 0 that 'sta (ptr),y' needs. Y is untouched, so the comment about Y surviving from the previous loop still holds. The rest of the window is already right and should not be touched: in particular 'inc ptr+1 / ldx ptr+1 / cpx #$0D / bne :-' deliberately uses X for the limit test because a 'lda ptr+1 / cmp #$0D' would destroy the A = 0 the fill loop depends on (rule 1/2).

assumption: Y is not live on entry to `solid` (it is not: the only jmp solid is from the SPRLINE k=0 arm, which never sets Y), and nothing between the stores reads Y.
original:
SOLID1 1
        SOLID1 2
        SOLID1 3
        SOLID1 4
        SOLID1 5
        SOLID1 6
        SOLID1 7
        jmp sprretP
; expands to, seven times:
;       ldy #k
;       lda (ptr),y
;       sta (sp),y
proposal:
ldy #1
        lda (ptr),y
        sta (sp),y
        iny
        lda (ptr),y
        sta (sp),y
        iny
        lda (ptr),y
        sta (sp),y
        iny
        lda (ptr),y
        sta (sp),y
        iny
        lda (ptr),y
        sta (sp),y
        iny
        lda (ptr),y
        sta (sp),y
        iny
        lda (ptr),y
        sta (sp),y
        jmp sprretP
argument: Cycle-neutral, byte-saving only. Original: 7 x (ldy #imm 2 + lda (zp),y 5 + sta (zp),y 6) = 91 cycles, 7 x 6 = 42 bytes. Proposal: ldy #1 (2) + 7 x (5+6) + 6 x iny (2) = 2 + 77 + 12 = 91 cycles, 2 + 7x4 + 6x1 = 36 bytes. Flags: the last instruction executed before the jmp is sta (sp),y in both, which sets no flags, so N,Z leaving the block come from the same final lda (ptr),y in both forms; the intermediate ldy #k / iny both set N,Z but those are dead. Y ends at 7 either way. No anonymous labels are added or removed. Page-crossing on (ptr),y is identical because the Y values are identical. Only worth taking because SPRFULL is instantiated several times, so it is 6 bytes per non-mirrored instantiation; if byte pressure is not an issue, leaving it alone costs nothing.

assumption: CHANGES THE ANONYMOUS LABEL COUNT -- one `:` is removed. See the warning in the argument.
original:
:       ldx #54
        bgt16 ox, px, :+
        bra :++
:       ldx #55
:       stx q1
proposal:
:       ldx #54
        bge16 px, ox, :+            ; px >= ox is exactly not(ox > px)
        ldx #55
:       stx q1
argument: bgt16 aa, bb forms bb - aa and branches on bmi, i.e. taken when aa > bb; bge16 aa, bb forms aa - bb and branches on bpl, i.e. taken when aa >= bb. So bge16 px, ox is taken exactly when px >= ox, which is the complement of bgt16 ox, px (taken when ox > px) -- the equality case lands on the ox <= px side in both readings, so X = 54 for ox <= px and 55 for ox > px, unchanged. Both macros expand to the same six-instruction shape (lda / cmp / lda / sbc / bvc :+ / eor #$80 / : / branch), so the prefix cost is identical and the signed-overflow correction is preserved -- this is a signed 16-bit comparison and stays one. Inverting the sense lets the branch jump straight over the ldx #55 and deletes the bra :++. Cycles: ox <= px goes from prefix + ldx 2 + not-taken branch 2 + bra 3 to prefix + 2 + taken branch 3, saving 2; ox > px goes from prefix + 2 + taken 3 + ldx 2 to prefix + 2 + not-taken 2 + ldx 2, saving 1. Two bytes saved. WARNING (rule 3): this removes one `:` line. The macro's own internal `:` sits before its final branch, so the :+ passed in still resolves to the label before stx q1 -- that part is safe -- but the earlier bra :++ in the @knocked block and any `:-` reference below stx q1 must be re-counted by hand before applying. The window's cost rank is 0, so this is a byte/tidiness change, not a speed one, and the label risk may not be worth taking.

assumption: fa is a zero-page symbol (3-cycle load); if it is absolute the saving is 4 cycles and 3 bytes.
original:
lda fa
        bmi @draw                   ; still dormant
        cmp #8
        bcs @draw
        ; rx > -8 && rx < (A+1)*2 && ry > -24 && ry < 8
        lda fa
        inca
        asl
proposal:
lda fa
        bmi @draw                   ; still dormant
        cmp #8
        bcs @draw
        ; rx > -8 && rx < (A+1)*2 && ry > -24 && ry < 8
        inca                        ; A is still fa: cmp does not write A
        asl
argument: The second lda fa is dead. cmp #8 compares without writing A, bmi and bcs are branches, and there is no label between the first load and the second (verified in src/logic.s 2683-2691: the only labels nearby are @nowrap above the first lda fa and @draw, which is the branch destination, not a fall-through point), so A still holds fa when the reload executes. Deleting it saves one zero-page load: 3 cycles, 2 bytes. Flags are unaffected in substance -- the deleted lda set N,Z from fa, but the very next instruction inc a overwrites both from its own result, and nothing between reads them. This is the whole finding for the window. The and #63 / eor #63 / clc / adc #129 sequence above it looks like it could lose the eor (and #63 / clc / adc #129 gives the same uniform range 129..192 in 6 cycles instead of 8) but that changes which random value maps to which dormancy delay, so it is a behaviour change, not a re-encoding, and I am not proposing it; every exact form of 192 - (r AND 63) costs the same 8 cycles.

assumption: A is dead after each mov16i -- it is: every one of the four is followed either by another mov16i, which reloads A, or by lda #TP_YOU / lda #TP_LOSE.
original:
@lose:  mov16i spx, 34
        mov16i spy, 4
        lda #TP_YOU
        jsr draw_piece
        mov16i spx, 80
        mov16i spy, 4
        lda #TP_LOSE
        jsr draw_piece
; mov16i expands to:
;       lda #<(imm)
;       sta dst
;       lda #>(imm)
;       sta dst+1
proposal:
@lose:  lda #34
        sta spx
        stz spx+1
        lda #4
        sta spy
        stz spy+1
        lda #TP_YOU
        jsr draw_piece
        lda #80
        sta spx
        stz spx+1
        lda #4
        sta spy
        stz spy+1
        lda #TP_LOSE
        jsr draw_piece
argument: Every immediate here is under 256, so mov16i's high half is lda #0 / sta dst+1 -- 2 + 3 = 5 cycles and 4 bytes where the 65C02's stz dst+1 does the same job in 3 cycles and 2 bytes. Two cycles and two bytes per occurrence, four occurrences in the window, so 8 cycles and 8 bytes; I am claiming 4 bytes to be conservative in case the assembler folds differently. Flags and registers: stz writes no flags, whereas the lda #0 it replaces set Z and cleared N. Those flags are dead at every one of the four sites -- each mov16i is followed by another lda # or by lda #TP_x. A is also left holding the low byte (34, 4, 80, 4) instead of 0, which is harmless for the same reason. The stores themselves are byte-for-byte identical in effect. The same change applies to the mov16i spx, 82 / mov16i spy, 4 pair in the @win arm just above this window. Cost rank 0 -- winlose draws once -- so treat this as a size win. The cleaner fix would be to teach mov16i to emit stz when the high byte is zero, which would pick up every call site in the codebase at once, but that is a macro change rather than a local re-encoding.

original:
@m80:   lda w16
        sta mulrowlo,x
        lda w16+1
        sta mulrowhi,x
        lda w16
        clc
        adc #ROWCHARS
        sta w16
        bcc :+
        inc w16+1
:       inx
        cpx #RINGROWS
        bne @m80
proposal:
@m80:   lda w16+1
        sta mulrowhi,x
        lda w16
        sta mulrowlo,x
        clc
        adc #ROWCHARS
        sta w16
        bcc :+
        inc w16+1
:       inx
        cpx #RINGROWS
        bne @m80
argument: The loop loads w16's low byte twice -- once to publish it into mulrowlo and once as the addend for the +80. Storing the high byte first leaves the low byte in A across `sta mulrowlo,x` (a store sets no flags and does not touch A), so the second `lda w16` is pure duplication and drops out: 3 cycles and 2 bytes per iteration, RINGROWS iterations, once at init. Correctness: the two table stores are to different arrays and are order-independent; `clc / adc #ROWCHARS` sees exactly the same A it saw before; `sta mulrowhi,x` and `sta mulrowlo,x` both use the same unmodified X; the carry into `bcc` still comes from the same `adc`; and no flags are live across the reorder (the first thing after each store is either another load or the `clc`). Anonymous labels unchanged. Cost rank 0 -- this is table setup -- so this is correctness-free tidying rather than a performance matter.

original:
lda fa
        bmi @draw                   ; still dormant
        cmp #8
        bcs @draw
        ; rx > -8 && rx < (A+1)*2 && ry > -24 && ry < 8
        lda fa
        inca
        asl
        eor #$80                    ; biased limit
        sta RNGTAB+49
proposal:
lda fa
        bmi @draw                   ; still dormant
        cmp #8
        bcs @draw
        ; rx > -8 && rx < (A+1)*2 && ry > -24 && ry < 8
        inca                        ; A still holds fa
        asl
        eor #$80                    ; biased limit
        sta RNGTAB+49
argument: fa is loaded, then tested twice, then loaded again. Neither test modifies A: `bmi` is a branch, and `cmp #8` sets N/Z/C from the comparison but leaves the accumulator alone -- that is the whole point of using `cmp` rather than `sbc`. So A still holds fa at the second `lda fa`, and the load is dead: 3 cycles and 2 bytes. The flags the deleted load would have set are immediately overwritten by `inca`, which is what `asl` and the rest actually read. Nothing between the two loads writes fa (there are no stores at all on the path, only branches). Neither branch target is entered between them -- both `bmi @draw` and `bcs @draw` leave the block entirely -- so there is no path that reaches `inca` without having just executed `lda fa`. Anonymous labels unchanged. The routine's cost rank is 0, so this is free tidying rather than a measurable win.

assumption: spx does not alias ox or fd (spx/spy are engine.s zero page reservations; ox = $A8, fd = $B2 in logic.s), and nothing reads spx between the two macros -- they are adjacent.
original:
mov16 spx, ox
        add16 spx, fd
proposal:
clc
        lda ox
        adc fd
        sta spx
        lda ox+1
        adc fd+1
        sta spx+1
argument: mov16 spx, ox expands to lda ox / sta spx / lda ox+1 / sta spx+1 (12 cycles, 8 bytes) and add16 spx, fd then expands to clc / lda spx / adc fd / sta spx / lda spx+1 / adc fd+1 / sta spx+1 (20 cycles, 13 bytes): spx is written, immediately read back, and written again. Adding straight out of ox into spx does both in one pass -- 20 cycles, 13 bytes -- saving 12 cycles and 8 bytes. The arithmetic is identical (spx = ox + fd, carry propagated from the low byte by the same clc/adc/adc chain), and the flags left behind are those of the final adc in both versions. It is only equivalent because spx is not itself a source: if fd aliased spx the original would compute ox + ox. They are distinct zero page variables. A is dead afterwards ('mov16 spy, oy' reloads it) and X, Y are untouched by either form. The identical pattern 'mov16 spy, oy / add16 spy, fc' appears two instructions above the window (logic.s:2361) and would save the same 12 cycles, but it is outside this window.

assumption: WINPX = ROWCHARS*2 = 160 (engine.s:110), a multiple of 8; and drawtext's entry is 'sta tx / stx ty', so it consumes no incoming flags.
original:
asl
        asl                         ; len*8
        sta tmp
        lda #WINPX
        sec
        sbc tmp
        lsr
        and #$FE
        jmp drawtext
proposal:
asl
        asl                         ; len*8
        eor #$FF                    ; WINPX - A, without parking A in memory
        sec
        adc #WINPX
        lsr
        jmp drawtext
argument:
Two changes.

(a) The subtraction is the wrong way round for the accumulator, so the code parks len*8 in tmp and reloads the constant: sta tmp (3) + lda # (2) + sec (2) + sbc tmp (3) = 10 cycles, 7 bytes. Complementing A instead gives the same result in 6 cycles, 5 bytes: eor #$FF makes 255-A, and 'sec / adc #WINPX' adds WINPX+1, for 256 + WINPX - A, i.e. WINPX - A modulo 256 -- exactly what the sbc produced, including its wrapping behaviour for oversized strings. tmp is left free rather than needing a value.

(b) 'and #$FE' is provably a no-op here. A is tya followed by three asl's, so it is a multiple of 8; WINPX is 160, also a multiple of 8; their difference modulo 256 is therefore a multiple of 8, and after the lsr the result is a multiple of 4, so bit 0 is already 0. Removing it saves 2 cycles and 2 bytes and changes no flag that matters: the and cannot alter Z (it only clears a bit that is already clear) and does not touch C, so drawtext sees the same N=0 (from lsr), the same Z, and the same C.

Total 6 cycles, 4 bytes. The only flag difference between the two versions is V (set by adc, previously by sbc); lsr and and both leave V alone, but drawtext starts 'sta tx / stx ty' and never branches on V, so it is dead.

assumption: Nothing reads t16 between the two macros (they are adjacent), and the value written is identical, so the `add16 t16, bvx` that follows is unaffected.
original:
mov16 t16, bvx              ; lda bvx / sta t16 / lda bvx+1 / sta t16+1
        asl16 t16                   ; asl t16 / rol t16+1
        add16 t16, bvx
proposal:
lda bvx
        asl
        sta t16
        lda bvx+1
        rol
        sta t16+1
        add16 t16, bvx
argument: mov16 writes t16 (12 cycles, 8 bytes) and asl16 then does a read-modify-write on both bytes it just wrote (asl zp 5 + rol zp 5 = 10 cycles, 4 bytes) - 22 cycles and 12 bytes to compute 2*bvx. Shifting in the accumulator on the way through costs lda(3) asl(2) sta(3) lda(3) rol(2) sta(3) = 16 cycles, 10 bytes: -6 cycles, -2 bytes. The carry chain is preserved exactly: `asl` on A leaves bit 7 of bvx in C, `sta t16` does not disturb C, `lda bvx+1` does not disturb C either (lda sets only N and Z), so `rol` shifts in the same bit that `rol t16+1` would have. Flags at the end differ - the block now ends on `sta` rather than `rol t16+1` - but the next instruction is add16's `clc`, which discards C, and N/Z are re-derived by its lda. The rest of the window resists: `asr16 t16` inside the `ldx #6` loop operates in place and has no mov16 to fuse with; `neg16 t16` cannot be merged into the later `add16 bvx, t16` as a `sub16`, because asr16 rounds toward minus infinity and negating before versus after the six shifts gives results that differ by one whenever 3*bvx is not a multiple of 64 - that would change the boomerang's motion, not just its encoding.

assumption: 9 cycles at each of the two sites (fc and fd), both on the same execution path, hence 18 per execution. t16 is scratch and nothing reads it between the mov16 and the asr16.
original:
mov16 t16, fc               ; lda fc / sta t16 / lda fc+1 / sta t16+1
        asr16 t16                   ; lda t16+1 / cmp #$80 / ror t16+1 / ror t16
        add16 rx, t16
        add16 spx, t16
        mov16 t16, fd
        asr16 t16
        add16 ry, t16
        add16 spy, t16
proposal:
lda fc+1
        cmp #$80                    ; C = sign bit of fc+1
        ror                         ; arithmetic shift of the high byte
        sta t16+1
        lda fc                      ; lda does not disturb C
        ror
        sta t16
        add16 rx, t16
        add16 spx, t16
        lda fd+1
        cmp #$80
        ror
        sta t16+1
        lda fd
        ror
        sta t16
        add16 ry, t16
        add16 spy, t16
argument: mov16 t16, fc costs 12 cycles / 8 bytes and asr16 t16 then re-reads and read-modify-writes what it just stored: lda t16+1(3) cmp #$80(2) ror t16+1(5) ror t16(5) = 15 cycles / 8 bytes, for 27 cycles and 16 bytes total. Shifting through the accumulator does the copy and the shift in one pass: lda fc+1(3) cmp #$80(2) ror(2) sta t16+1(3) lda fc(3) ror(2) sta t16(3) = 18 cycles, 12 bytes. -9 cycles, -4 bytes, twice in this window. The arithmetic is identical to the macro's: `cmp #$80` sets C to 1 exactly when the high byte is >= $80, i.e. to the sign bit, and the first `ror` shifts that sign back into bit 7 while dropping the high byte's bit 0 into C, which the second `ror` then shifts into bit 7 of the low byte - the same two-byte rotate the macro performs, just with A standing in for the memory operand. The one subtle point is that `lda fc` between the two rotates must not clobber the carry: `lda` affects only N and Z on the 6502/65C02, so the carry survives. Flags on exit are also identical - the block ends on `sta t16`, which sets nothing, leaving the N/Z/C of the final `ror`, precisely what `ror t16` would have left - and in any case the next instruction is add16's `clc`. fc and fd are read, never written, so sourcing the shift directly from them is safe.

assumption: Neither C nor V is consumed between here and @drawc - verified, @drawc's first instruction is `clc`.
original:
jsr shr16x
        lda w16
        and #3
        clc
        adc #4
        bra @drawc
proposal:
jsr shr16x
        lda w16
        and #3
        ora #4
        bra @drawc
argument: `and #3` leaves A in 0..3, so bit 2 is guaranteed clear and adding 4 is exactly setting it: `ora #4` (2 cycles, 2 bytes) replaces `clc / adc #4` (4 cycles, 3 bytes). -2 cycles, -1 byte. The `clc` is genuinely needed in the original because `and` does not touch the carry, which arrives from whatever shr16x's last `dex/bne` or `lsr/ror` left, so this removes a real dependency rather than a redundant one. Flags: `adc` sets N, Z, C and V; `ora` sets only N and Z, and to the same values since the result is identical. The C and V it no longer sets are dead - control falls to `@drawc: clc / adc #TP_CLEO0`, which clears the carry itself before using it. The @lframe arm reaches @drawc with its own `and #3` and is untouched. Note the two additions cannot be merged into one `ora`, because TP_CLEO0 may share bits with the 0..7 frame index and only the `+4` is provably disjoint.

assumption: A is dead immediately after `ror w16` (it is: the next instruction on either path is `lsr sp_rinc` then `lda sp_col`).
original:
bne :+
        lda w16+1
        cmp #$80
        ror w16+1
        ror w16
        lsr sp_rinc
proposal:
bne :+
        lda w16+1
        asl
        ror w16+1
        ror w16
        lsr sp_rinc
argument: This is an inline `asr16 w16` (arithmetic shift right of a signed 16-bit value). The idiom uses `cmp #$80` purely to copy bit 7 of A into the carry so that the following `ror` re-injects the sign. `asl` (accumulator) does the same thing - it shifts bit 7 of A into C - in the same 2 cycles but in 1 byte instead of 2. Both set N and Z from a result nobody reads. The only flag consumed is C, by `ror w16+1`, and both instructions leave C = bit 7 of w16+1, so the shift is bit-identical. A differs afterwards (w16+1 doubled versus w16+1 unchanged), which is why the assumption above matters: the next flag/A consumer is `lsr sp_rinc`, which reads neither, and then `: lda sp_col` reloads A. This is a bytes-only win; the cycle count is unchanged, which is why I have not touched the surrounding code. The rest of the window is already minimal: the 16-bit add `sp_rp = sp_col + w16` cannot drop its `clc` because on the `bne :+` path the carry comes from `and #2` (unaffected) back through `sbc sp_lb0+1`, i.e. it is not reliably clear, and the `sec / sbc` computing sp_ncol needs its `sec` for the same reason. The signed shift itself cannot become `lsr w16+1 / ror w16`: w16 here is sp_r0*8 - sp_lb0 computed with `lda #0 / sbc sp_lb0+1`, which is genuinely negative whenever sp_lb0 > 0.

original:
mov16 t16, bvx
        add16i t16, 128
        lda t16+1
        sx16 t16
        add16 bx, t16
proposal:
lda bvx
        cmp #$80                    ; C = bit 7 of bvx = carry out of (bvx + 128)
        lda bvx+1
        adc #0                      ; A = high byte of bvx + 128
        sx16 t16
        add16 bx, t16
argument: This computes bx += (bvx + 128) >> 8 sign-extended, i.e. a rounded divide by 256. The low byte of bvx + 128 is computed, stored into t16, and then thrown away, because `sx16 t16` expands to `sta t16 / and #$80 / beq :+ / lda #$FF / : sta t16+1` and its first instruction overwrites t16 with A. So the entire 16-bit add's low half is dead, and the only thing needed from it is the carry into the high byte. Original cost: `mov16 t16, bvx` = lda/sta/lda/sta = 12 cycles, 8 bytes; `add16i t16, 128` = clc/lda/adc/sta/lda/adc/sta = 18 cycles, 13 bytes; `lda t16+1` = 3 cycles, 2 bytes - 33 cycles and 23 bytes in total before sx16. The replacement is 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10 cycles and 8 bytes, saving 23 cycles and 15 bytes. Correctness of the carry: bvx + 128 carries out of the low byte exactly when bvx >= 128, i.e. when bit 7 of bvx is set, and `cmp #$80` sets C = 1 iff A >= $80, which is that bit. `lda bvx+1 / adc #0` then produces the same high byte the full add16i produced. `lda t16+1` is also gone because A already holds that byte - in the original it was a reload of what `sta t16+1` had just written, and in the new form it is what `adc #0` leaves in A. sx16 consumes only A (its first instruction is `sta`, which sets no flags, and its second is `and #$80`, which sets its own), so the flags differing between `lda t16+1` and `adc #0` are dead. t16's low byte was never read before sx16 overwrote it, and t16+1 is written by sx16, so dropping both stores is safe; `add16 bx, t16` then reads the pair sx16 wrote, unchanged. bvx is zero page (logic.s:226) and t16 is $D1, so all the cycle figures above are zero-page timings. Two things I deliberately did NOT propose. (1) The `ldx #6 / : asr16 t16 / dex / bne :-` loop above could be replaced by `asl16 t16` twice plus a sign-extend of the high byte, which would cut about 86 cycles - but that requires t16 << 2 not to overflow 16 bits, and t16 here is -3*bvx while bvx is initialised to -3584 at logic.s:1472, so -12 * bvx overflows badly. Unsafe. (2) Unrolling that same loop saves 31 cycles for 35 bytes and removes an anonymous label; a fair trade but a separate judgement from this one.

assumption: A and the flags are dead at @ydir - verified: @ydir begins `bpl16 ry, @rypos`, which expands to `bit ry+1 / bpl`, and `bpl` reads N from ry+1 while the Z that `bit` derives from A is never tested; both successors then start with a fresh `lda`.
original:
bpl16 rx, @rxpos
        blt16 fc, fa, :+
        bra @ydir
:       inc fc
        bne @ydir
        inc fc+1
        bra @ydir
@rxpos: beq16 rx, @ydir
        beq16 fc, @ydir
        bmi16 fc, @ydir
        lda fc
        bne :+
        dec fc+1
:       dec fc
proposal:
bpl16 rx, @rxpos
        bge16 fc, fa, @ydir
        inc fc
        bne @ydir
        inc fc+1
        bra @ydir
@rxpos: beq16 rx, @ydir
        lda fc+1
        bmi @ydir
        ora fc
        beq @ydir
        lda fc
        bne :+
        dec fc+1
:       dec fc
argument: Two independent changes. (1) `blt16 fc, fa, :+ / bra @ydir / :` branches over a branch. `bge16` expands to the identical five-instruction signed compare and differs only in ending `bpl label` instead of `bmi label`, so `bge16 fc, fa, @ydir` tests the exact complement and the `bra` disappears: fc >= fa falls from 15 + bmi not taken 2 + bra 3 = 20 to 15 + bpl taken 3 = 18 (saving 2), and fc < fa falls from 15 + bmi taken 3 = 18 to 15 + bpl not taken 2 = 17 (saving 1), reaching `inc fc` by fall-through. Both forms do the full signed 16-bit compare with the V correction, so this is not the unsigned-comparison trap. (2) `beq16 fc, @ydir / bmi16 fc, @ydir` together mean 'branch if fc <= 0', but they test the low byte first and then re-read the high byte: beq16 is lda fc / ora fc+1 / beq (8 cycles when it falls through) and bmi16 is bit fc+1 / bmi (5). Testing the sign first from a single load gives the same predicate - fc < 0 iff bit 7 of fc+1, and otherwise fc == 0 iff fc+1 | fc == 0 - in `lda fc+1 / bmi @ydir / ora fc / beq @ydir`. That is 10 cycles when neither branch is taken, against 13 (saving 3), and 6 when fc is negative, against 14 (saving 8). It costs 2 cycles in the single case fc == 0, where it walks both tests instead of exiting on the first; I judge that the minority case for a chase variable, but it is the reason this is marked medium rather than high. A at @ydir becomes fc+1 or fc+1|fc rather than fc|fc+1, which the stated assumption covers. Bytes: 2 for the deleted `bra`, 2 for the shorter sign test. WARNING on anonymous labels: change (1) deletes the `:` in front of `inc fc`. I grepped logic.s 2390-2450 and ob_bat contains no `:-` at all - every anonymous reference in the routine is a forward `:+` resolving to a later `:` (the `lda fc / bne :+ / dec fc+1 / : dec fc` pattern and its fd twin), so removing this one retargets nothing. Verify in the listing. Note the identical `blt16 fd, fb, :+ / bra @boom` construct appears a few lines later for the Y axis and takes the same treatment.

assumption: A is dead after ob_powerup returns - the rewrite leaves A = fa>>1 rather than fa on the `bcs @done` exit taken from @draw. The other entry to @done (`@adv: cmp #6 / bcs @done`) is unchanged and still leaves A = fa, so the two exits already disagree today only in that both were fa; if the dispatcher reads A after the rts this is not safe.
original:
@draw:  lda fa
        cmp #6
        bcs @done
        lsr
        clc
        adc #97
        jmp m_addsprite
@done:  rts
proposal:
@draw:  lda fa
        lsr
        cmp #3
        bcs @done
        adc #97
        jmp m_addsprite
@done:  rts
argument: Doing the halve before the range test makes the test itself produce the clear carry that `adc #97` needs, so the `clc` goes away. The bound is preserved exactly: fa >= 6 iff (fa >> 1) >= 3 for unsigned fa, and fa is unsigned and bounded at 6 here (it is set to 1 on pickup and the `@adv: cmp #6 / bcs @done` gate above stops `inc fa` past 6), so there is no edge case at the boundary - fa = 5 gives 2 which is below 3, fa = 6 gives 3 which is not. The carry into `adc` is correct because `cmp` sets C = 1 iff A >= operand, so falling through `bcs @done` guarantees C = 0, exactly what the deleted `clc` was providing. Note the `lsr` must move above the `cmp`, not merely have the `clc` deleted - `lsr` sets C from bit 0 of fa, which alternates, so in the original order the `clc` is genuinely load-bearing. The sprite id computed is unchanged: (fa >> 1) + 97. 2 cycles and 1 byte, on a cost-rank-0 path, so this is a tidy-up rather than a win; I have flagged it medium only because of the A-on-exit question in the assumption, which is not answerable from inside the window.

original:
lda w16
        and #3
        clc
        adc #4
        bra @drawc
proposal:
lda w16
        and #3
        ora #4
        bra @drawc
argument: `and #3` leaves A in 0..3, so bit 2 is guaranteed clear and adding 4 can never carry into it from below - the add is therefore exactly a bit set, and `ora #4` produces the identical 4..7 result in 2 cycles and 2 bytes instead of `clc / adc #4`'s 4 cycles and 3 bytes. Saving 2 cycles and 1 byte. Flag differences are all dead: `adc` writes N, Z, C and V while `ora` writes only N and Z, but the result is in 4..7 in both cases so N = 0 and Z = 0 either way, and the carry is not consumed because the branch target @drawc opens with its own `clc` before `adc #TP_CLEO0`. (V likewise is never tested - there is no `bvc`/`bvs` on this path.) The `bra @drawc` is unaffected. Note this is the win-screen arm; the lose arm at @lframe ends `lda w16 / and #3` and falls straight into @drawc with no add, so it needs no change and the two arms stay consistent. The rest of the window - the `lda #$79 / sta w16 / lda #$9E / sta w16+1 / lda #$E7 / sta w16b` constant load feeding shr24x, and the `and #30 / tax` shift-count computation - is already minimal, and at cost rank 0 (menu animation) none of it is worth further risk.

assumption: X is dead across the bvy multiply (the next use of X is the ldx #6 three instructions later). D=0, as everywhere in this file.
original:
mov16 t16, bvx
        add16i t16, 128
        lda t16+1
        sx16 t16
        add16 bx, t16
        mov16 t16, bvy
        asl16 t16
        add16 t16, bvy
        neg16 t16
        ldx #6
proposal:
lda bvx
        clc
        adc #128
        lda bvx+1
        adc #0                      ; A = high byte of bvx + 128
        sx16 t16
        add16 bx, t16
        lda bvy
        asl
        tax                         ; X = 2*bvy low, C untouched by tax
        lda bvy+1
        rol
        sta t16+1
        txa
        clc
        adc bvy
        sta t16
        lda t16+1
        adc bvy+1
        sta t16+1                   ; t16 = 3*bvy
        neg16 t16
        ldx #6
argument: Two savings. (1) mov16 t16,bvx (12) + add16i t16,128 (18) + lda t16+1 (3) = 33 cycles, 23 bytes, and every byte it writes to t16 is dead: sx16 immediately overwrites t16 with A and t16+1 with the sign. Worse, the lda t16+1 is pure waste - add16i's last instruction is sta t16+1, so A already holds that byte. All that is wanted is the high byte of bvx+128 in A: lda bvx / clc / adc #128 / lda bvx+1 / adc #0 = 12 cycles, 11 bytes. sx16 t16 then stores the identical pair, and add16 bx,t16 is untouched. Saving 21 cycles, 12 bytes. (Substituting cmp #$80 for clc / adc #128 would save 2 more - cmp #$80 sets C exactly on the carry out of bvx+$80 - but the clc form is the conservative one.) (2) mov16 t16,bvy + asl16 t16 + add16 t16,bvy is 42 cycles and 25 bytes to build 3*bvy through memory. Doubling in the accumulator and keeping the low half in X is 34 cycles and 21 bytes for the same result: TAX leaves C alone, so the carry out of asl reaches the rol that forms the high byte, and the add of bvy back in starts from a fresh clc. Saving 8 cycles, 4 bytes. Anonymous labels: sx16's single ':' is preserved because sx16 itself is kept, and neg16/asl16/add16/mov16 contain none, so the ':' of the asr16 countdown below and every :+ / :- in this routine keep counting to the same places. The same (1) rewrite applies verbatim to the by half a few lines below this window, for another 21.

original:
@rxpos: beq16 rx, @ydir
        beq16 fc, @ydir
        bmi16 fc, @ydir
        lda fc
        bne :+
        dec fc+1
:       dec fc
...
@rypos: beq16 ry, @boom
        beq16 fd, @boom
        bmi16 fd, @boom
        lda fd
proposal:
@rxpos: beq16 rx, @ydir
        lda fc+1
        bmi @ydir
        ora fc
        beq @ydir
        lda fc
        bne :+
        dec fc+1
:       dec fc
...
@rypos: beq16 ry, @boom
        lda fd+1
        bmi @boom
        ora fd
        beq @boom
        lda fd
argument: beq16 fc,label followed by bmi16 fc,label reads fc+1 twice: lda fc (3) + ora fc+1 (3) + beq (2) for the zero test, then bit fc+1 (3) + bmi (2) for the sign test = 13 cycles, 10 bytes. Testing the high byte first lets one load serve both: lda fc+1 (3) + bmi (2) + ora fc (3) + beq (2) = 10 cycles, 8 bytes. Saving 3 cycles and 2 bytes per site. Correctness: the combined condition is 'fc <= 0'. The new form branches on N of fc+1, which is the same bit bit/bmi tested; if that bit is clear, fc+1 is non-negative, so fc+1 OR fc is zero exactly when the 16-bit value is zero - identical to beq16. A is left holding fc+1|fc instead of fc|fc+1 (the same number) and is dead anyway: the next instruction is lda fc. No anonymous label is added or removed, so the bne :+ / :+ pairing below is untouched. The window contains two such sites - the x chase at @rxpos and the y chase at @rypos - and they lie on independent halves of the routine, so a call that takes both positive branches saves 6; each site alone saves 3. The blt16 fd,fb,:+ / bra @boom pairs are left alone: blt16 defines its own anonymous label, so touching them would retarget the caller's :+.

original:
@draw:  lda fa
        cmp #6
        bcs @done
        lsr
        clc
        adc #97
        jmp m_addsprite
@done:  rts
proposal:
@draw:  lda fa
        lsr
        cmp #3
        bcs @done                   ; not taken: C = 0 for the adc
        adc #97
        jmp m_addsprite
@done:  rts
argument: The clc exists only because lsr clobbers C with bit 0 of fa. Halving before the range test removes the need for it: fa >= 6 iff fa>>1 >= 3 (fa=5 gives 2, fa=6 gives 3, and any larger byte gives 3 or more), so cmp #3 on the halved value makes exactly the same decision, and falling through bcs @done guarantees C = 0 for the adc. Original: lda (3) + cmp #6 (2) + bcs (2) + lsr (2) + clc (2) + adc (2) = 13 cycles, 10 bytes. Proposal: lda (3) + lsr (2) + cmp #3 (2) + bcs (2) + adc (2) = 11 cycles, 9 bytes. Saving 2 cycles, 1 byte. The sprite id reaching m_addsprite is unchanged (97 + fa/2), @done is rts and consumes no flag, and the other bcs @done above the window (from @adv's cmp #6) is untouched.

original:
sta tmp2
        mov16i spx, 66
        mov16i spy, 28
        lda tmp2
        jsr draw_piece
proposal:
sta tmp2
        lda #66
        sta spx
        stz spx+1
        lda #28
        sta spy
        stz spy+1
        lda tmp2
        jsr draw_piece
argument: mov16i expands to lda #<imm / sta dst / lda #>imm / sta dst+1. Both immediates here are under 256, so each macro spends lda #0 (2) + sta (3) = 5 cycles and 4 bytes on a high byte that stz writes in 3 cycles and 2 bytes. Two macros: 20 cycles and 16 bytes become 16 cycles and 12 bytes, saving 4 of each. stz sets no flags where lda #0 set Z - but the next instruction in each case is another immediate load or a load of tmp2, so nothing reads them. spx/spy get the identical 16-bit values. I left the lda tmp2 reload alone: caching A in X or Y across the four stores would cost 4 cycles against the 3 the reload costs. This is the win/lose screen (cost rank 0), so the value here is code size as much as time.

assumption: None. RINGLO and RINGHI are independent arrays, so the order of the two stores is free.
original:
@r:     lda w16
        sta RINGLO,x
        lda w16+1
        sta RINGHI,x
        lda w16
        clc
        adc #<ROWBYTES
        sta w16
proposal:
@r:     lda w16+1
        sta RINGHI,x
        lda w16
        sta RINGLO,x
        clc
        adc #<ROWBYTES
        sta w16
argument: The loop loads w16's low byte, stores it, destroys A with the high byte, then reloads w16 to start the add. Storing the high byte first leaves the low byte in A at exactly the point the add needs it, deleting one `lda w16` - 3 cycles and 2 bytes per iteration, x RINGROWS. Correctness: RINGLO,x and RINGHI,x are distinct locations so swapping the two stores is observationally identical; `sta` sets no flags so the `clc` that follows is unaffected either way, and `clc` is kept because the previous iteration's `adc #>ROWBYTES` can leave carry set. A on entry to `adc #<ROWBYTES` is w16's low byte in both versions. Flags on exit from the block are set by `sta w16` (none) in both, and the loop tail `inx / cpx #RINGROWS / bne @r` sets its own. No anonymous labels involved. This is once-per-init code (cost rank 0), so the value is code size and tidiness rather than frame time.

assumption: Two, both verifiable from macros.txt and the window: (1) neg16 ends with `lda #0 / sbc var+1 / sta var+1`, so it leaves A = t16+1; (2) t16's low byte is dead between `mov16 t16, bvy` and `sx16 t16`, because sx16 expands to `sta t16 / and #$80 / beq :+ / lda #$FF / sta t16+1` and therefore overwrites both bytes.
original:
neg16 t16
        ldx #6
:       asr16 t16
        dex
        bne :-
        add16 bvy, t16
        asl16 ry
        add16 bvy, ry
        mov16 t16, bvy
        add16i t16, 128
        lda t16+1
        sx16 t16
        add16 by, t16
proposal:
neg16 t16                   ; leaves A = t16+1
        ldx #6
:       cmp #$80
        ror
        ror t16
        dex
        bne :-
        sta t16+1
        add16 bvy, t16
        asl16 ry
        add16 bvy, ry
        lda bvy                     ; only the high byte of bvy+128 is ever used
        clc
        adc #128
        lda bvy+1
        adc #0
        sx16 t16
        add16 by, t16
argument: Two independent dead-work removals. (A) The asr16 loop reloads t16+1 from memory and shifts it in memory on every one of six passes. neg16 has just left that byte in A, so the high half can stay in A for the whole loop: `cmp #$80` sets carry from the sign exactly as before, `ror` (A) performs the same arithmetic shift and leaves the same carry (bit 0 of the old high byte) for `ror t16`. Per iteration 3+2+5+5+2+3 = 20 becomes 2+2+5+2+3 = 14; six iterations 119 -> 83, plus a single `sta t16+1` (3) on exit = 86, a 33-cycle saving and 1 byte. Nothing between the iterations reads t16+1, so its staleness during the loop is unobservable, and X is the counter in both versions. (B) `mov16 t16, bvy / add16i t16, 128 / lda t16+1` builds a full 16-bit sum whose low byte is never read - the very next thing, `sx16 t16`, writes t16 from A and t16+1 from the sign, discarding both bytes of the sum. Only the carry out of the low addition matters, so the low half needs no store: `lda bvy / clc / adc #128 / lda bvy+1 / adc #0` (12 cycles) replaces 12+18+3 = 33, saving 21 cycles and 14 bytes. Carry on exit is the carry out of bvy+1+0+c in both versions (sx16's `and`/`beq`/`lda`/`sta` leave C alone), and `add16 by, t16` begins with `clc` anyway, so even that does not matter. Flags: the loop now falls out of `bne` with Z set from `dex` and then executes `sta t16+1`, which sets none - identical to before; the following `add16` starts with `clc / lda`. Anonymous labels: unchanged, one `:` in the loop, still the target of `bne :-`. Note the identical pattern appears in the bvx half immediately above (logic.s:1636-1643) and the same two rewrites apply there for another 54 cycles.

assumption: A need not survive the test. Visible in the window: @boom is reached with A = fd (fall-through after `dec fd`), with A from `inc fd+1`, and from two `bra @boom` sites with entirely different values, so `jsr boomready` cannot depend on A. Carry is likewise not an input - boomready sets it, and `bcc @player` reads what boomready returned.
proposal:
@rypos: beq16 ry, @boom
        lda fd+1
        bmi @boom
        ora fd
        beq @boom
argument: The fd pair means `branch if fd <= 0` and loads fd+1 twice. `lda fd+1` sets N from bit 7 exactly as `bit fd+1` did, so `bmi @boom` is unchanged; on fall-through A already holds fd+1, so `ora fd` yields the same fd|fd+1 that `lda fd / ora fd+1` yielded. Swapping the order of the ==0 and <0 tests is harmless because both go to the same label. Cycles on the fall-through path (which continues into the 16-bit decrement): 3+3+2+3+2 = 13 becomes 3+2+3+2 = 10; the bmi-taken path is 6 either way and the beq-taken path 14 -> 11. Bytes 10 -> 8. The `beq16 ry` above is left alone - ry is a different variable and cannot be merged. The only behavioural change is that `bit` preserved A and `lda` does not, covered by the assumption. No anonymous labels are added or removed. The same three-test pattern at @rxpos (logic.s:2416-2418, on rx/fc) admits the identical rewrite for another 3 cycles.

assumption: @done does not read A or N. Verified: within ob_vanish `@done:` is a bare `rts`. This is the one fact outside the window the rewrite needs.
original:
@count: inc fe
        lda fe
        and #3
        bne @done
        lda fe
        cmp #12
proposal:
@count: inc fe
        lda fe
        bit #3
        bne @done
        cmp #12
argument: `and #3` destroys A, which forces the `lda fe` reload on the fall-through path. On the 65C02 immediate BIT sets Z from A AND the operand and - uniquely among the BIT modes - leaves N and V alone, so `bit #3` gives `bne @done` the identical Z while preserving A = fe. The reload then disappears: 2+3 = 5 cycles for `and #3`+`lda fe` becomes 2 for `bit #3`, saving 3 cycles and 2 bytes (and the subsequent `cmp #12 / bcs :+ / lsr` chain runs on the same fe it would have loaded). The difference is what reaches @done on the taken path: previously A = fe&3 (non-zero) with N clear, now A = fe with N and V as `lda fe` left them. Since @done is `rts` and its caller re-derives everything, nothing consumes either. C is untouched by `bit #imm`, and the first flag-consumer on the fall-through is `bcs :+` reading the new `cmp #12`. No anonymous labels involved.

assumption: Nothing reads t16 or t16+1 between the add16i and the sx16 -- visible in the window, the only instruction between them is the redundant load itself. sx16's first instruction is 'sta dst', which is what makes add16i's low-byte store dead.
original:
add16i t16, 128
        lda t16+1
        sx16 t16
        add16 by, t16
proposal:
clc                         ; t16 += 128, keeping only the high byte
        lda t16
        adc #128
        lda t16+1                   ; low result is dead: sx16 overwrites t16
        adc #0
        sx16 t16                    ; A is already the high byte
        add16 by, t16
argument: add16i t16,128 expands to clc / lda t16 / adc #$80 / sta t16 / lda t16+1 / adc #0 / sta t16+1, and sx16 t16 expands to sta t16 / and #$80 / beq :+ / lda #$FF / : sta t16+1. Three instructions are provably dead. (a) add16i's 'sta t16' writes the low byte, and the very next thing to touch t16 is sx16's own 'sta t16', which overwrites it -- nothing reads it in between, so the store is dead (3 cycles, 2 bytes). The adc itself must stay: it produces the carry into the high byte. (b) The explicit 'lda t16+1' reloads a byte the accumulator already holds, because add16i finished with 'sta t16+1' and sta does not alter A (3 cycles, 2 bytes). (c) With that load gone, add16i's 'sta t16+1' is also dead: the only consumer was that load, and sx16 rewrites t16+1 unconditionally at its end (3 cycles, 2 bytes). Total 9 cycles, 6 bytes. Correctness: 'lda t16+1' between the two adc's does not disturb carry (lda affects only N and Z), so the carry produced by 'adc #128' still reaches 'adc #0' exactly as before. A entering sx16 is the same high byte in both versions, so the sign-extension and the resulting t16 pair are identical, and 'add16 by, t16' sees the same operand. Flags: sx16 starts with a store and then does its own 'and #$80', so no flag crosses the boundary. Registers X and Y are untouched. Anonymous labels: none added or removed -- sx16's internal ':' is unchanged and add16i has none. Worth noting for a wider window: the preceding 'mov16 t16, bvy' (line 1652, just outside) is then dead too, since its 'sta t16' is overwritten by sx16 and its 'sta t16+1' by sx16's tail; sourcing the adc chain from bvy directly would save a further 12 cycles.

assumption: Only the carry flag is consumed after the plp. I checked the fall-through: 'bcc @player' is the sole flag reader, and the code it falls into is 'jsr @kill / lda #8 / sta bcnt', which sets its own flags. If some future edit makes N, V or Z live across this point the php/plp would have to come back.
original:
ldx #28
        jsr inrange
        php
        mov16 rx, t16
        mov16 ry, t16b
        plp
        bcc @player
proposal:
ldx #28
        jsr inrange
        mov16 rx, t16               ; lda/sta do not touch carry
        mov16 ry, t16b
        bcc @player
argument: The php/plp pair exists to carry inrange's result flag across the two restores. But mov16 expands to lda / sta / lda / sta, and on the 6502/65C02 neither lda nor sta writes the carry flag -- only N and Z (and only lda writes those). So the carry returned by inrange survives the eight instructions between the php and the plp untouched, and the save/restore is pure overhead: php is 3 cycles 1 byte, plp is 4 cycles 1 byte, total 7 cycles and 2 bytes removed. The bcc then reads exactly the same carry it reads today. The one behavioural difference is N/Z/V: plp restores inrange's N, Z and V, whereas without it the flags in force are those left by the final 'lda t16b+1' of the second mov16. The window plus the surrounding source shows the only flag consumer is the bcc itself, and both successors ('@player: lda health' and the fall-through 'jsr @kill / lda #8') begin by setting their own flags, so nothing observes the difference. plp also restores I and D, which nothing here depends on. Registers are untouched (X is the inrange argument and is dead after the call; the mov16s use only A). No anonymous labels change.

assumption: None: the carry state is established by the 'bcc @six' immediately above, inside the window.
original:
:       cmp #37
        bcc @six
        lda #48
        sec
        sbc fe
        lsr
        bra @set
proposal:
:       cmp #37
        bcc @six
        lda #48
        sbc fe                      ; carry is already set: bcc fell through
        lsr
        bra @set
argument: Falling through 'bcc @six' means the branch was not taken, which by definition means carry = 1 from the 'cmp #37'. The intervening 'lda #48' is an immediate load and does not alter carry (lda writes only N and Z). So the borrow is already in the state sec would force, and the sec is redundant: 2 cycles and 1 byte removed. The subtraction 48 - fe therefore produces the identical result, and the following lsr shifts the same value. Flags: sec would set carry to 1, which it already is, so the sbc sees an identical input state and leaves identical N, V, Z and C; the lsr then overwrites carry anyway and 'bra @set / sta q1' consumes nothing. Registers are untouched. No anonymous labels change -- the ':' shown is the existing target of the 'bcs :+' above and is not moved. Also examined: reordering the three arms so one of the two 'bra @set' jumps falls through would save 3 cycles on the fe >= 37 arm but costs 3 on the 12 <= fe < 37 arm, so it is distribution-dependent and left alone.

assumption: tmp2 need not survive item_y. The rewrite only stops writing it, so any caller that had a live value in tmp2 is strictly better off; the sole use of tmp2 in item_y is the one being removed. X is already clobbered by item_y today (ldx tmp2), and the call site at menu.s:326 does jsr item_y / tax, so it wants only A. No anonymous labels are added or removed: beq :++ still counts forward past the loop-head ':' to the ':' on the rts.
original:
item_y: sta tmp2
        lda mtop
        ldx tmp2
        beq :++
:       clc
        adc mstep
        dex
        bne :-
:       rts
proposal:
item_y: tax
        lda mtop
        cpx #0
        beq :++
:       clc
        adc mstep
        dex
        bne :-
:       rts
argument: The parameter is already in A and is wanted in X, so the round trip through tmp2 (sta tmp2 3 / lda mtop 3 / ldx tmp2 3 = 9 cycles, 6 bytes) can be a register transfer. tax cannot simply carry its own Z through, because lda mtop sits between it and the branch and overwrites N/Z (rule 1) - hence cpx #0 to regenerate Z from X without disturbing A. That gives tax(2) lda mtop(3) cpx #0(2) = 7 cycles / 5 bytes. cpx #0 also forces C = 1, which is harmless: the loop body opens with clc before the adc, and on the taken path the next instruction is rts with C dead. The count semantics are unchanged - X holds the same value it did before and the dex / bne loop is untouched. A dex-and-bmi pre-decrement variant would be the same 7 cycles but would add an unnecessary signed assumption on the item count, so I have not proposed it. Cost rank 0, so this is bookkeeping rather than a win worth disturbing the file for on its own.

assumption: q1 <= 9. Verified at logic.s:3014: div10_16 builds the remainder in q1 by the shift-and-conditional-subtract method (rol q1 / lda q1 / cmp #10 / bcc / sbc #10 / sta q1), so q1 is reduced below 10 on every one of the 16 iterations and is a true 0..9 remainder on return. No anonymous labels are touched.
original:
@d:     phx
        jsr div10_16
        plx
        lda q1
        clc
        adc #'0'
        sta numbuf,x
        dex
        bpl @d
proposal:
@d:     phx
        jsr div10_16
        plx
        lda q1
        ora #'0'
        sta numbuf,x
        dex
        bpl @d
argument: '0' is $30 and q1 is 0..9, so q1 occupies only bits 3..0 and $30 only bits 5..4 - the two operands are bit-disjoint and q1 + $30 is identically q1 | $30, with no carry ever generated out of any bit position. That turns clc(2) + adc #'0'(2) into ora #'0'(2), saving 2 cycles and 1 byte. Flags: adc set N, Z, C and V; ora sets only N and Z. The three dropped-flag consumers are checked - sta numbuf,x affects nothing, dex regenerates N and Z for the bpl that follows, and neither C nor V is read anywhere before the next clc-free path (the leading-zero loop below starts with ldx #0 / lda numbuf,x / cmp #'0', which sets its own carry). The loop runs 5 times per draw_number call, so the call-level saving is 10 cycles. If q1 could exceed 9 the rewrite would be wrong (e.g. 10 | $30 = $3A rather than $3A - which happens to coincide, but 22 | $30 = $36 vs 22 + $30 = $46 does not), which is why the div10_16 bound is stated explicitly rather than assumed.

assumption: None. A is clobbered by both versions (bmi16 leaves A alone but beq16 immediately overwrites it), and @nostomp begins 'lda hurt'.
original:
bmi16 vy, @nostomp
        beq16 vy, @nostomp
        jsr @kill
proposal:
lda vy+1                    ; N from the high byte, exactly what bmi16's bit did
        bmi @nostomp
        ora vy                      ; then Z from vy|vy+1, exactly what beq16 built
        beq @nostomp
        jsr @kill
argument: bmi16 expands to 'bit vy+1 / bmi' and beq16 to 'lda vy / ora vy+1 / beq'; back to back they load vy+1 twice. 'lda vy+1' sets N from bit 7 of vy+1, which is precisely the N that 'bit vy+1' set, so the bmi is unchanged. Falling through it, A holds vy+1, and 'ora vy' produces vy+1|vy -- the same value, and therefore the same Z and N, as beq16's vy|vy+1. Cycles on the fall-through path: 3+2+3+2 = 10 against 3+2+3+3+2 = 13, saving 3; bytes 2+2+2+2 = 8 against 2+2+2+2+2 = 10, saving 2. On the bmi path A is vy+1 instead of untouched, dead because @nostomp opens with 'lda hurt'. Neither bmi16 nor beq16 contains an anonymous label, so the ble16i above (which does, via its bvc :+) is unaffected and the label count is unchanged. The combined test still means 'skip unless vy > 0 signed', with the sign taken from the high byte and the zero test over both bytes, exactly as before.

assumption: A is dead after the test -- confirmed: both paths reach '@next1: inc level / lda level', which reloads it.
original:
lda level
        and #1
        bne @next1
        inc level
@next1: inc level
proposal:
lda level
        lsr                         ; C = bit 0
        bcs @next1
        inc level
@next1: inc level
argument: 'and #1 / bne' and 'lsr / bcs' both branch exactly when level's bit 0 is set, and lsr is the one-byte accumulator form against and #'s two. Cycles are identical (2 each). Correctness: lsr leaves A = level>>1 and sets C from the discarded bit 0, Z from the shifted result and N clear; the original left A = level&1 with Z from it. The branch consumes C in one and Z in the other, both correctly, and everything else is dead -- the target and the fall-through both continue with 'inc level' (a memory RMW that does not read A) followed by 'lda level'. Level is a plain unsigned counter, so no signed comparison is involved. A byte-only win, reported because it is free.

assumption: X and A on return from music_init are dead (the new loop exits with X=0 and A=MUSIC_ADDR[0] rather than X=144 and A=MUSIC_ADDR[143]); music_init is called once, from main.s:96. Also assumes the copy direction does not matter - source and destination are in different banks (MUSIC_ADDR=$B800 in BANK_TIL1, music_tab in main RAM), so they cannot overlap.
original:
ldx #0
:       lda MUSIC_ADDR,x
        sta music_tab,x
        inx
        cpx #144
        bne :-
        rts
proposal:
ldx #144
:       lda MUSIC_ADDR-1,x
        sta music_tab-1,x
        dex
        bne :-
        rts
argument: Counting down lets DEX set Z directly and removes the 'cpx #144' (2 cycles, 2 bytes) from every iteration. The -1 bias on both bases is needed because the loop must stop at X=1, so X runs 144..1 and addresses MUSIC_ADDR+143..MUSIC_ADDR+0 - the same 144 bytes, in reverse. 'ldx #143 / dex / bpl' would be wrong: 143 has bit 7 set, so BPL fails on the very first test. The cycle arithmetic is not the naive 2/iteration: MUSIC_ADDR is $B800 (engine.s:3175), page-aligned, so the original 'lda MUSIC_ADDR,x' with x=0..143 never crosses a page, while the new 'lda MUSIC_ADDR-1,x' has base $B7FF and crosses into $B8xx on every access, costing +1. Net is 16 -> 15 cycles per iteration, i.e. 144 cycles over the loop, plus 2 bytes. The store side is unaffected: 'sta abs,x' is a fixed 5 cycles with no page-cross penalty. This is cold init code (rank 0, called once at startup), so the saving is real but immaterial; flagged as an improvement for completeness rather than because it is worth churning the source for. Confidence is medium only because the exit-state assumption on X and A is outside the window.

assumption: A is dead on entry to @nostomp. Verified in logic.s: @nostomp begins 'lda fc', overwriting A immediately. The V flag set by the original 'bit ry+1'/'bit vy+1' is also dead: @nostomp's first flag consumer is 'cmp #2' and the fall-through path's is 'cmp #2' as well, neither reading V.
original:
bmi16 ry, @nostomp
        beq16 ry, @nostomp
        bmi16 vy, @nostomp
        beq16 vy, @nostomp
proposal:
lda ry+1                    ; ry <= 0 ?
        bmi @nostomp
        ora ry
        beq @nostomp
        lda vy+1                    ; vy <= 0 ?
        bmi @nostomp
        ora vy
        beq @nostomp
argument: bmi16 expands to 'bit var+1 / bmi' and beq16 to 'lda var / ora var+1 / beq', so each pair costs bit zp (3) + bmi (2) + lda zp (3) + ora zp (3) + beq (2) = 13 cycles and 10 bytes on the fall-through. Because the two macros test the same variable back to back, the high byte can be loaded once: 'lda ry+1' sets N from bit 7 exactly as 'bit ry+1' does, so the bmi is unchanged; then 'ora ry' leaves A = ry|ry+1, which is zero iff the 16-bit value is zero - exactly the Z that beq16 computes, just with the operands in the other order (OR is commutative). That is lda (3) + bmi (2) + ora (3) + beq (2) = 10 cycles, 8 bytes. Saves 3 cycles and 2 bytes per pair, 6 and 4 for the two pairs. The one behavioural difference is that BIT preserves A whereas LDA does not, so on the path where the first bmi is taken A is now clobbered - harmless here because @nostomp's first instruction is 'lda fc' (see assumption). The other difference is V: BIT copies bit 6 of the operand into V, LDA leaves V alone; V is not read on any successor path. Carry is untouched by lda/ora/bit alike. On the full fall-through path the final A and Z are identical to the original (same OR of the same two bytes). No anonymous labels are involved - neither bmi16 nor beq16 contains a ':'.

assumption: A is dead on entry to @nostomp - verified: '@nostomp: lda hurt' overwrites it immediately. V from the original 'bit vy+1' is dead too: @nostomp's next flag consumer is the 'bne' fed by 'lda hurt'.
original:
ble16i ry, 4, @nostomp
        bmi16 vy, @nostomp
        beq16 vy, @nostomp
        jsr @kill
proposal:
ble16i ry, 4, @nostomp
        lda vy+1                    ; vy <= 0 ?
        bmi @nostomp
        ora vy
        beq @nostomp
        jsr @kill
argument: Same fusion as logic_2134, applied to the one variable that is tested twice here. 'bmi16 vy / beq16 vy' is bit vy+1 (3) + bmi (2) + lda vy (3) + ora vy+1 (3) + beq (2) = 13 cycles, 10 bytes; loading the high byte once gives lda vy+1 (3) + bmi (2) + ora vy (3) + beq (2) = 10 cycles, 8 bytes. 'lda vy+1' sets N from bit 7 just as 'bit vy+1' does, so the sign test is unchanged; 'ora vy' produces the same OR (commutative) and hence the same Z for the zero test. Saves 3 cycles and 2 bytes whenever the sign test does not fire (the bmi-taken path is 6 cycles either way). A is clobbered on the bmi-taken path where BIT would have preserved it, and V is no longer set from bit 6 of vy+1 - both dead (see assumption). Carry untouched throughout. The ble16i above is left alone: its bvc/eor #$80 sequence is a signed comparison and must not be turned into an unsigned bcc/bcs. No anonymous labels added or removed (bmi16/beq16 contain none; ble16i's single ':' is untouched).

assumption: A and Y are dead on entry to draw_glyph_rows. Verified in menu.s:87 - it begins 'lda tx / lsr / sta w16 / stz w16+1 / lda ty / lsr / lsr / jsr m_ringaddr / ldx #0', so it establishes A, X and (inside m_ringaddr) its own state, and never reads the incoming A or Y. The '@space' path it falls to afterwards reloads Y with 'ldy tchar'. Costs 14 bytes.
original:
ldy #7                      ; '_' = erase: draw an all-zero glyph
        lda #0
@z:     sta GLYPHBUF,y
        dey
        bpl @z
        jsr draw_glyph_rows
proposal:
stz GLYPHBUF+0              ; '_' = erase: draw an all-zero glyph
        stz GLYPHBUF+1
        stz GLYPHBUF+2
        stz GLYPHBUF+3
        stz GLYPHBUF+4
        stz GLYPHBUF+5
        stz GLYPHBUF+6
        stz GLYPHBUF+7
        jsr draw_glyph_rows
argument: GLYPHBUF is 8 bytes in the TABLES segment (engine.s:230), i.e. absolute, not zero page - so STZ abs applies at 4 cycles / 3 bytes each. The loop costs ldy #7 (2) + lda #0 (2) + seven iterations of sta abs,y (5) + dey (2) + bpl taken (3) = 70, plus a final 5 + 2 + 2 = 9, for 83 cycles in 10 bytes. Eight straight STZs are 32 cycles in 24 bytes: 51 cycles saved for 14 bytes spent. The stores are to the same eight addresses with the same value, so the memory effect is identical. What is lost is the loop's exit state - A = 0 and Y = $FF - and the N/Z it leaves; all dead (see assumption). This is the '_' erase path in menu text drawing, so it is cold; the trade is offered because the metric ranks cycles above bytes, but on a byte-tight build it is reasonable to decline. If bytes matter more, unrolling by two ('ldy #6 / lda #0 / : sta GLYPHBUF,y / sta GLYPHBUF+1,y / dey / dey / bpl :-') gives 67 cycles for 6 extra bytes - note that variant ADDS no anonymous label only if @z is reused rather than replaced by a ':'.

assumption: Y is 0 on exit from the second 256-byte loop - it must be, since that loop exits precisely when 'iny' wraps Y to 0 and the bne is not taken. The 1634 figure is per iteration of the outer @r loop, which runs 28 times, so roughly 45,750 cycles per call to clear_items. Costs about 25 bytes.
original:
ldy #0
        lda #0
:       sta (w16),y
        iny
        bne :-
        inc w16+1
:       sta (w16),y
        iny
        bne :-
        inc w16+1
        ldy #0
:       sta (w16),y
        iny
        cpy #128
        bne :-
proposal:
ldy #0
        lda #0
:       sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        bne :-
        inc w16+1
:       sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        bne :-
        inc w16+1
                                    ; Y is already 0: the loop above exited on the wrap
:       sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        sta (w16),y
        iny
        cpy #128
        bne :-
argument: Two changes. (1) The third 'ldy #0' is dead: the loop immediately above it ends with 'iny / bne :-', which can only fall through when iny has wrapped Y to $00, and the intervening 'inc w16+1' does not touch Y. Deleting it saves 2 cycles and 2 bytes per outer iteration; the Z=1/N=0 it set is dead too, because the next instruction is 'sta (w16),y', which sets no flags, and the first flag consumer after that is the loop's own bne fed by iny. (2) Unrolling each loop four ways amortises the branch. Per byte the original is sta (w16),y (6) + iny (2) + bne (3) = 11 for the two 256-byte loops and 13 for the 128-byte one (it pays an extra cpy #128). Unrolled by four, a group is 4*(6+2) + 3 = 35 cycles for 4 bytes (8.75/byte) and 4*(6+2) + 2 + 3 = 37 for the counted loop (9.25/byte). Totals per outer iteration: loop 1 2815 -> 2239, loop 2 2815 -> 2239, loop 3 1663 -> 1183; with the ldy that is 1634 cycles saved for about 25 bytes (three extra sta/iny pairs per loop at 3 bytes each, less the 2 for the ldy). The unroll is exact, not approximate: 256 and 128 are both multiples of 4, so the loops still terminate on precisely the same Y values (0 by wrap for the first two, 128 for the third) and the same byte counts are written - no over- or under-run past the 640-byte ring row. ANONYMOUS LABEL NOTE: the proposal keeps exactly three ':' labels, the same as the original, so nothing counting past this block is retargeted. This is menu code (rank 0, one call per menu open), so the absolute saving is large but cold; the ldy #0 deletion alone is free in both cycles and bytes and is worth taking regardless.
